utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Judge Kamenova will be absent briefly in morning for urgent personal reasons. She should join us later in the course of the session. We've decided that it's in the interests of justice to continue in her absence, and in fact I think it may be the first time we've sat in her absence. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're ready to proceed with General Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're going to continue with your evidence. We're still with Mr. Hannis asking questions. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, General. When we left off on Friday, we were talking about Exhibit P2592; it was an excerpt from your diary regarding the May meeting. I think you have a hard copy on your desk. Friday I asked you about Mr. Milosevic's reference to the cases of big Serbs and asking that those be resolved. One question I have for you: Was the murder of Fehmi Agani mentioned during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I think the last question I asked you on Friday was who Saja was and you told us that referred to Mr. Sainovic. Under the reference to Saja, there's a mention of: "And there's the task of working on cleaning up the terrain." Can you tell us what that referred to, as discussed in this meeting.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cleaning of the terrain is actually an expression for mopping up the remaining Siptar terrorist groups on the ground, on the terrain. That is a professional military term used in military terminology anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is there a similar term that refers to removing bodies from the battle-field?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is mop-up of the battle-field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there any discussion of that during this 17 May meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just mentioned briefly that asanacija or mop-up or sanitization of the terrain should be completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, the last two questions I think I have for you concerning this diary entry are near the bottom. There's a reference to Rade, and it apparently says: "There are no groups of five to 100 with the tendency to form bigger groups." I'm not sure if that translation is correct, but can you tell us what that refers to.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a problem as to whether larger groups had been dealt with, whether those were their numbers, actually, that is the figure that General Pavkovic gave. And Milosevic reacted to that when he made a remark regarding to what the military spokesperson said to the media; namely, that not all remaining groups in the territory had been cleaned up yet. And in relation to that, Milosevic said that such unbalanced statements should be -- should not be made because it would give NATO a pretext to enter Kosovo and things should be dealt with differently. Rade Markovic minimised the remaining number of groups and he also said that they were smallish groups, that there were perhaps five to 100 people on such groups. So he said that these were small remaining groups and the military spokesperson had said that there were pockets in the terrain consisting of larger groups of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So that's a reference to KLA groups or terrorist groups?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you read your original entry because it says,"Rade said there are no groups of five to 100," and that doesn't seem to make sense to me.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably there was a discussion before that, and I did not write that down. But these were groups consisting of five to 100 persons and then he is saying that there are no such groups at all. So the thesis expounded by Rade Markovic was that all groups had been cleared up; that was Milosevic's point of view, too; and then there was the problem of the military spokesman who said to the media something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I understand. Finally, there's a reference to Jugoslav Petrusic. I think you mentioned his name earlier, but can you tell us who he was and why he was detained.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jugoslav Petrusic is a French citizen of Yugoslav origin who sometime in the 1970s had emigrated to France, and later on he became a member of the French DST intelligence service. He was used primarily, according to what the existing knowledge shows, for assassinations. He came to Yugoslavia immediately after the conflict with NATO started in 1999. He established a group of 25 persons, and through certain connections he managed to go very quickly through the procedure through the centre in Grocka for taking in volunteers. He was sent to the 125th Brigade. He was at the Albanian border; and since the State Security Service of Serbia had information to the effect that this was a French agent or French agents, Milosevic ordered that this entire group be withdrawn from Kosovo and that Petrusic and Orasanin be withdrawn -- be arrested. They were, actually, withdrawn and a trial took place. They were in custody for 30 days. They were under military jurisdiction, but both the office of the military prosecutor and of the civilian prosecutor were consulted, and it was assessed that there weren't sufficient grounds for bringing charges, criminal charges. A decision was made to expel him seven days later, then the State Security Service arrested him. And they wanted to draw -- to turn this into a scandal saying that he was planning an assassination against Milosevic and so on and so forth, but actually it was aimed against the military service but this was in actual fact handled by the civilian state security. When prosecution witnesses were supposed to appear, they refused. And the case ended with very small punishment for illegal entry into the country or something like that, but certainly it had nothing to do with the original charges and what was said in the media campaign in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us on Friday how at this meeting Rade Markovic had made the remark that volunteers were a necessary evil. Did -- when he made that remark in the meeting, did anyone disagree with him or take issue with that statement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. This position was one that Rade Markovic took after I presented information about Arkan's group, the 30 men of Arkan's who were in Kosovo Polje and then this group of Slobodan Medic, Boca, the Skorpions that is; that is the context in which he said they were a necessary evil and that they are accompanying this war but that 100 volunteers does not resolve the question of war. That's it. No one had a position that was different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, the -- the group of 25 volunteers that Petrusic enrolled or got together, were they Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly. I could not say with any degree of certainty. Most of them were and some were returnees. I know that some of them were in the 10th Sabotage Detachment and had waged war in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what was the ground for thinking that their interests would be anti-Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The State Security Service -- well, we had detained Petrusic and Orasanin as the key people in that group who had actually avoided the procedure of going through the Grocka centre; however, when the decision was made for the two of them to be expelled from Yugoslavia, after that they were arrested by the State Security Service, they were held in detention for a longer period of time, and they had allegedly confessed during that detention that they were preparing an assassination against Milosevic. There was a lot of pressure brought to bear and a lot of forged statements. One of the persons from that group, for instance, claimed in connection with me that during the war in 1999 that I had been in Moscow with him in 1999 in order to purchase weapons. So there were quite a few lies bandied about and these people were forced to make various statements. These statements were actually given under duress. I cannot say what is true, what is not true. I just know that as far as court proceedings are concerned nothing was actually proven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what's the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to identify who that individual was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wasn't interested in the particulars of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, General, where did you go after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that meeting I returned to the security administration, if you're talking about that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you recall what time of day that meeting was and when the meeting concluded, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it started - if I'm not mistaken - sometime around 10.30. I'm not sure about the actual time. I don't know whether I have it written down somewhere. Perhaps I can look through this material, but I'm not certain of the time. At any rate, it is late in the morning, and perhaps it went on until 1.00. It did not go beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say, in paragraph 71 of your statement, that as you left Mr. Milosevic asked Mr. Sainovic and Rade Markovic to stay behind. You say that you felt that was inappropriate. Can you tell us why you thought it was inappropriate for him to ask them to stay behind.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it has to do with two things. First of all, at the meeting, General Pavkovic and General Ojdanic somewhere towards the end accentuated the need to establish a mixed joint state commission which should establish what it was that was going on in Kosovo. Milosevic avoided commenting on that at all. He turned the tables on everyone, saying that there was not proper communication between the civilian and the military services. So this proposal remained sort of hanging in the air; it was unresolved. I personally think that when this kind of a joint meeting is brought to an end, it is not right to keep someone there longer after the meeting is over. You said Sainovic and Rade Markovic and that is what Milosevic said. No he just said to Rade Markovic: "Rade, you stay," and Mr. Sainovic stayed, too. To say the least, my impression was that he was kept there in order to have a subsequent discussion but without us; that was my impression and that is the comment I made to Mr. Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on now to paragraph 75 in your statement, where you talk about your June trip to Kosovo that you and Colonel Gajic and Colonel Antic went to Kosovo the 1st through the 7th of June with a task to carry out a fact-finding commission about some of the alleged crimes that you had been informed about in May. In paragraph 76, you say that while travelling around you saw widespread destruction in the rural areas. Can you tell the Court what was the nature of that damage. Were you able to draw some conclusion about how it had occurred based on what you saw.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's quite difficult to present a general picture. We were moving along roads. There were damaged buildings along the way, and also the bridge, for instance, near Gornja Klina across the Beli Drim River. It seemed empty, an empty space in these rural areas; that's the impression I had, with a lot of dead animals, livestock, that had not been dealt with. They were lying by the roads, and these houses by the road were destroyed. Now, I cannot say whether it was due to air attack or artillery attacks. For the most part, they were destroyed and there were only walls and chimneys left, practically no roofs. However, I cannot say anything with certainty as to what had caused the damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then you tell us while you were in Pristina in paragraph 77 and 78, that General Pavkovic invited you to a meeting of a group that you later were told by Pavkovic was the Joint Command. And you detail who the persons attending were; and in paragraphs 80 through 82, you talk further about what was discussed. I had a question for you about Mr. Andjelkovic. Did he say or do anything during this meeting you attended?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He attended the meeting and he was there, like the rest of the persons there. He did not take part in the discussion because I certainly would have made a short note of that in the notebook that I had with me, and I did write down what the participants in the discussion said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have trouble hearing the witness. Could all other microphones be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you notice, was anyone taking notes of the meeting during the meeting other than yourself that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Every one of the participants had a notebook or a pad of his own. But if you're asking about an official record-keeper, I did not see any; that is to say, there weren't any. Now, as for the individuals that were writing notes of their own and whether they had any notes that they made before that in order to speak on the basis of those notes during the meeting, that I don't know, but they all had their own notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 83, you mention that Stojanovic told you that Jovica Stanisic had been involved in the work of the joint commission in 1998 for several months. Did he say when he stopped participating in the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. He just said that in passing, that during a longish period of time of their work, Jovica Stanisic took part as well, but there were no details mentioned for how long, why, and in what period, that is. Since he was retired in October 1998, it probably had to do with the summer months.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 86, you say that you prepared a report that you submitted to your boss, General Farkas, about what you and Gajic had learned on your fact-finding mission. Have you ever seen that report since you submitted it to General Farkas?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. There was no need for me to see it after that. This report was compiled on the 7th of June, immediately upon our return. It had been typed out; it consisted of certain tables, too. And I already mentioned that on the following day, the 8th, General Geza handed the report over to General Ojdanic and that General Ojdanic ordered that the same report be sent on to President Milosevic. It remained in the safe of the chief of the administration. Now, what happened after that when we were retired, or rather, when we were removed from these positions, first of all, that is the end of March/beginning of April 2000. I don't know about that. I know that later I had expressed an interest to get it, too. And I remember that at the time General Ojdanic was looking for the report, too, or rather, he was looking for it later when he was preparing his defence. He was still free, but the report could not be found. It's -- it really doesn't contain anything that anybody would have an interest in concealing or destroying and it did refer to court cases as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in paragraph 87, you say that you and Gajic documented 42 cases of crimes, some by the VJ and some by the MUP. Can you tell us, was that one individual per case, or did sometimes a case involve more than one individual? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. In some cases two or three members of the army participated. For instance, a crime, a murder, that was committed in the village of Bresje where three reserve members of the military killed an Albanian and mistreated another Albanian. So it is one single case, but three perpetrators. And there are other such cases, too. Also, there are many cases that refer to individual cases. For instance, a case of a particular Captain Stekovic who killed four Albanians, raped a girl; so it's one perpetrator and several victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember the largest number of perpetrators associated with one case? Was there any case where there was a group bigger than two to three perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there were. It pertains to the tactical group of the 52nd Armoured Brigade. So there were cases of three or four individuals, but not of an entire unit, a squad, a platoon, et cetera, having committed something like that. Usually, it was three or four persons; two or three, four reservists who would go out together and usually they would be under the influence. Sometimes they would drink alcohol and then do something. They would commit rape, looting, or even killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of the 42 cases, do you recall how it broke down between the MUP and the VJ? Was it about equal? Were there twice as many on one side as the other? Do you recall what the numerical breakdown was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give any accurate figures. I'm sure of one thing, that most of the cases that we dealt with were cases that pertained to the military. As for the MUP cases, it was more or less a general report and we did not go into any of the details concerned because it did not fall within our jurisdiction. I would like to say that these 42 cases are not all killings or murders. There are killings and murders, there are rapes, and also many cases of lootings, robbery, taking property from abandoned houses. So it did not pertain strictly to killings and murders, crimes of that kind. We also had information about misdemeanours, but also about big crimes. But we put it all together and presented it in a table.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did this group of 42 cases include the murder of Fehmi Agani?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just mentioned there because there was a report security organ providing us with this information, and this information was included in our table.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it you envisage the Trial Chamber doing with this information?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, part of the reason I'm trying to elicit this information is to see if we can -- if we can locate this document or document that we believe to be this document, I'll have a sufficient description of it from this witness to confirm that what I have is probably what he's been talking about; also to see if the information that he's referring to as having reported up the line on that date is referred to in other collections or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if these -- if these events aren't referred to in the indictment, what's the relevance of them for our purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it would be part of our argument that there was a reporting system in place and that sometimes, relatively speaking, very minor events worked their way up to the top to -- of the VJ and they were discussed in the VJ collegium, et cetera; yet, on the other hand, some significant events with dozens if not hundreds killed did not seem to get reported. And there's an argument we may make from that at the end of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The four specific locations referred to there are said to have been mentioned above somewhere in the statement. Not this minute, but can somebody perhaps identify for me at least the particular paragraphs that these four locations are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would ask the General's assistance with that, Your Honour, because I'm not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps someone on your behalf can go through this and remind us where these are referred to so we can tie this in later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I can come back to you on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, now, I want to ask you regarding those 42 cases, do you personally know the results or the outcome of any of those in terms of prosecutions?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports that we received from the security organs as far as these were concerned, all the cases, the prosecutions were brought against those people, I don't know if any of them received the first-instance judgements. I don't know about the final outcome as far as the judicial organs are concerned. The only case that was not prosecuted was the case in Gornja Klina. This is something I've already spoken about in the jurisdiction of the 37th Brigade, and this case referred to a killing, I think, of seven Albanians who were then thrown into a well and then the -- some soil was thrown over it. When we were there at what time, there was no prosecution in this case. An on-site investigation was attempted, but at that time Gornja Klina was already under Albanian control so it was not possible to access this area. I know that this case ended up at the military court in Nis because the commander of that unit was involved - that was a logistics battalion - and this officer was prosecuted. I don't know what the final outcome was. I know that there was some other cases of active-duty servicemen who were tried after the state of war ended and they were tried in Nis. But I wanted to make a note here lest one should draw a conclusion that we went down there as some sort of a supervisory commission, me and Gajic. We went there to visit the security organs, to carry out the usual control into their work, and we also, on the orders of General Ojdanic, wanted to check out what the situation was, what we could learn on the ground. And I think that the military prosecutors and the military courts have the full information about all this. We did not confer with them. We did not compare our data with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. General, during proofing and preparation of your written statement, you make reference in paragraph 89 about being asked about the murders listed in Schedules A through K of the indictment in this case. And you indicated that the only one that you had information about related to Izbica. And I understand from earlier in your statement, you did not believe those 120- or 30-some bodies that were dug up there related to the total number of 800. Is it correct that you had no information about the other killings referred to in the indictment in this case? Bela Crkva, Orahovac, Krusevac, or Meja?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I maintain what I said. It was not 120, 130, but it was 143 bodies that were buried individually in the cemetery, and we were told that orders had been given for those bodies to be exhumed and that the area should be sanitized. I don't know what hospital was in charge there, whether it was Kosovska Mitrovica, but the pathologists were supposed to examine the bodies and the investigating judge should have gone out and conducted an on-site inquiry. I don't know under what circumstances these people died, whether it was in the fighting or whether these were actual killings. This is as regards the 143 bodies. As for the other locations, no reports were received, but you have to bear in mind that we didn't spend a lot of time in Kosovo. I'm just giving you the information we received from security organs in certain areas. Now, whether these locations were in their locations, I don't know about that. They did not mention anything about that. Had they known about it, they would have given us information because they had given us information about many other serious cases. So I don't know why they would miss those.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you visit the security organs in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We did not have a security organ in place in Orahovac. As for Djakovica, I've already mentioned this, I gave you the name of the lieutenant from the 252nd Rocket Brigade. This rocket brigade was deployed in artillery battalions over a pretty wide stretch. It was a brigade that was supposed to do the air defence. So in Orahovac there was no security organ in place. I don't know whether there was one in this zone of responsibility or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am familiar with this area of Suva Reka because I had been there in the past. As far as I remember, there is a place called Musitiste there. And I remember that the security from the 70th military territorial detachment reported no problems in the detachment, and that in Musitiste there was an elderly Albanian man who was given meals by the military and the military was generally taking care of this man. So this was the only information I had from Suva Reka, but that was in Musitiste. The 70th detachment was in Musitiste as they were feeding this elderly [Realtime transcript read in error "earlier"] Albanian. As for Suva Reka, I don't know whether we had any of our units there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about two more, Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Vucitrn or Vushtrri?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We didn't have any security organs in place there. There may have been some, but I didn't go there and the security chief in the 3rd Army was with me. And he, in fact, defined our route, the route that we would take, because we could not have visited all the security organs because there were quite a few of them. We were supposed to get a general picture on the basis of the key points, the Pristina Corps, the brigades that were part of that corps. We went all the way down to military territorial detachments and battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In line 18, the word "earlier" should be "elderly," in case it's not picked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I heard, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 90, you say that on 9th of July there was finally a follow-up meeting with the MUP as envisioned at the 17th May meeting, and you say that Minister Stojiljkovic indicated that only 16 MUP members were being processed for crimes. Did he tell you what kinds of crimes those 16 were being processed for?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wanted to tell you that General Geza and General Ojdanic, after the meeting in May, tried to get in touch with Rade Markovic in order to hold this meeting about the alleged problems in the cooperation, but it was impossible to get in touch with him. This meeting was finally held on the 8th of July or maybe 9th of July. I'm not quite sure about the date, but it was one of the two. The entire interior ministry top was there, the Serbian interior ministry. The meeting was held in the headquarters, and General Ojdanic presided and Vlajko Stojiljkovic was there. And I found it peculiar that only 16 cases were prosecuted, but this was the kind of meeting where the cases themselves were not discussed at all. The crimes were not on the agenda. The discussion centred on the casualties, the MUP and military personnel that were killed or wounded. They said the situation was quite good because they only had the 16 cases. I personally believe that those were the severe cases because there must have been more cases that were prosecuted for lesser crimes, because I find it hard to believe that only 16 cases -- that that would be the total number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there was no connection between those 16 cases and the 326 bodies that had been determined to have been found in the area under the responsibility of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This figure was not mentioned at all. The agenda was completely different for this meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones kindly be switched off while the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the second time a request has been made about switching off microphones, but I can't see any switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I've been guilty a time or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you're entitled to keep yours on, Mr. Hannis, as long as you're not shuffling papers beside it and I don't see any more on. So I'm sorry, I don't think we can help the interpreters any more on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, two last things, two last areas I want to cover with you. The VJ collegium, do you know what that was? Can you explain to the Judges what the VJ collegium was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The collegium consists of the closest associates and immediate subordinates of the Chief of General Staff or some other commander. You can have a collegium of an army commander or a corps commander. So those would be the closest associates dealing with the key sectors important for the functioning of a command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1998 and 1999, were you aware of whether the VJ collegium existed at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was not the collegium of the Yugoslav army. This is not a proper term. You can have a collegium of the Chief of General Staff as the operational commander of the Yugoslav army. So there is no such thing as the collegium of the Yugoslav army. There is the collegium of the Chief of General Staff. It had been in existence in 1990s and later on. So when I retired it existed, when I was reinstated it existed, and it exists now. This is a permanent body.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the early 1990s, before your first retirement, did you participate in the collegium of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The chief of military security is always a member of the collegium. At that time it was, in fact, the federal secretary of national defence, General Kadijevic, but the Chief of General Staff, General Adzic, had his own collegium. So it is a collective body composed of the heads of various sectors in the military organisation, and they discuss certain issues and the commander makes the final decision on any issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you say the chief of military security is always a member. I thought you were second to the chief of military security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999, Your Honour. In the early 1990s, he was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm sorry. Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999, did your boss, Geza Farkas, attend the General Staff collegium meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1999, when he was actually appointed the head of the security administration until he was removed from this office, he was a member of the collegium and he did attend the meetings of the collegium. There may have been some exceptions when he was absent officially and then somebody else would attend the meeting in his stead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know how often it met in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Approximately? Was it once a year? Once a month?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, definitely not once a year. I think it was, in fact, more often than once a month. It would depend on the actual need, but on the average perhaps every ten days or so there would be a meeting, depending on the importance of the issue to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your preparation for testimony this week and last week, did you have occasion to review some minutes of VJ collegium meetings from late 1998 and early 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was shown those minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see the list of attendees at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you recognise those individuals named as being members of the General Staff or holding the positions that were indicated in the list of attendees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know where this examination will take us, but I'm afraid that we're now re-visiting the situation we had on the first day when the Prosecutor tried to tender through this witness documents from a meeting that this witness did not attend, a meeting that this witness has no direct knowledge of from the time when he was actually not on active duty. I don't know how far the Prosecutor intends to go, but I would like to lodge an objection because I think that we are now in the same situation that we had before and I believe that the Trial Chamber has already ruled on the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If the witness was being asked to deal with the events which were said in the minutes to have taken place at the meeting, that would be one thing, Mr. Visnjic, and your objection may have some foundation on that. But here all he's being asked is to say what positions the people who, according to the minutes, attended the meeting held. And that's something within his competence, bearing in mind the position he held and his experience of this body and, therefore, we'll allow that question to be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, my question was: Did you recognise those individuals named as being members of the General Staff or holding the positions that were indicated on that list of attendees?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did recognise the -- practically all of the names on this list, and there are actually more of them listed there than I remember from the collegium that I attended in the early 1990s and 1980s. There were maybe eight or nine generals there, and now there were more than ten people. But it is up to the Chief of General Staff to decide who would attend the collegium. It is not something that is strictly stipulated in the rules that -- which heads of which services are to be represented, although there are some that have to be represented and that are always represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think I have one more question I want to ask you relating to -- regarding the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I have a moment, Your Honour. I'm locating my binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you a couple of names. Do you know who David Gajic was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know the name. He was the chief of the state security department in Kosovo in 1997/1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what about a Milan Djakovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him, too. He was a general in the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In 1998, do you know where he was stationed or what his command was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was in the Pristina Corps command. First he was the -- while General Pavkovic was the commander and then later on, he was the chief of the operations division in the 3rd Army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any more questions. No, I'm sorry. I don't have any more questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order will be: Mr. Sainovic, General Ojdanic, General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, General Lukic, and Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is it Mr. Fila or Mr. Petrovic who's going to lead out?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be cross-examining the witness, but it is the view of myself and all the other Defence teams that we need to know which documents will be admitted into evidence, because you know that we objected -- made certain objections regarding the use of some documents by the Prosecution, the minutes and so on, and we need your decision. Because when I examine Mr. Vasiljevic, I have to know this. Because if the documents are admitted, then I will examine him in one way; and if not, then I will do it in another way. Or if you do not wish to rule on that, then you should give me the right to re-examine him. I think that may be a problem because the Chamber is not sitting in its full composition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what is your position in relation to the various documents to which objection was taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've -- we still think that they're appropriate to be considered. I can make some oral arguments this time. I can make a written submission later concerning the relevance, but as I indicated most of them were documents received pursuant to RFAs or have indicators of reliability. And I think I can tell you which ones in my list of the notification I'm not seeking to admit at the conclusion of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: P1011, P2591, and, Your Honour, all the others I'm seeking to introduce. Some for the reason that they were associated with his testimony in Milosevic, and I can give you those cross-reference numbers if you would like. It's extensive. Perhaps I can submit that to you in writing at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are there exhibits from Milosevic which are not included in the numbers to which exception was taken at the beginning of this witness's evidence? Because if there are, you haven't given us numbers relative to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think they took exception to just about everything. The one might be P2593, which is an organisational chart that was shown in private session in Milosevic, relating to the security service. I think -- I think all the others there were objections to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's take, as an example, the very first document that was listed by Mr. Petrovic, P928. Can we have that, please, on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is one of the VJ General Staff collegium minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next page, please. The record should also reflect now that Judge Kamenova has come on to the bench. The next page, please. The next. And the final page, please. The Defence assumption, Mr. Hannis, is that you seek to exhibit this document to rely on its contents. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. May I make some additional submission regarding why I think it should come in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I indicated before, these were received from Serbia and Montenegro in response to a request for assistance for these specific items. Based on -- in part of the evidence of this witness, we have established the existence of such a body with these members at this point in time. The listed participants, and the contents themselves, we would argue further suggest they're authentic. Likewise, with the contents, there is what I would call "good stuff" for both the Defence and the Prosecution, which I submit also further suggests authenticity. It's not completely one-sided one way or the other. And, finally, Mr. Visnjic in the list of documents that he's submitted to us as Defence exhibits he intends to discuss with this witness, include another five or six VJ collegium minute sessions that were not on my list. So it appears he has some belief that they were authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Fila, I'm assuming from all that's been said that from 928 to 941 are documents of a similar nature, and 928 is simply an example of a series of documents which are said to be minutes of the collegium. Mr. Hannis has not asked the witness to put any gloss on the documents; he simply asked the witness questions which seek to establish the authenticity of the documents. He's saying that the contents are for later argument or, indeed, for exploration in cross-examination. He's can't deny you that possibility. Now, are you challenging the authenticity of these documents? Mr. Petrovic's original challenge was based on the fact that there was no link between the witness and the documents, and that I can understand in relation to any questions that might have been asked of this witness to explain them, but that hasn't happened. So the question we're looking at at the moment is: Do you dispute their authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that my colleague Mr. Visnjic is using them, I do not challenge their authenticity, and I do not intend to question the witness in relation to these documents. The objection raised by Mr. Petrovic is of a principled nature and concerns all documents. Why was this document not introduced through any other witness who knows as much about them? So let us agree on the documents to be tendered between the two sides. I'm interested in some other documents, but I'll raise that issue later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept any decision Your Honours make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does any other Defence counsel challenge the authenticity of these particular ones? I'm going to move to the others that were listed in a moment. All right. Now, the next category that Mr. Petrovic challenged were described as a variety of documents about the military and the police. The circumstances in relation to three of these are now rather different from the time he made his submission. The Prosecutor does not seek to exhibit P2591, and as we indicated earlier I think P1427 and P1960 are already exhibits in the case. Now, again Mr. Hannis has not tried to seek any explanation of these documents from the witness. That statement may be too general. I'm not sure if perhaps one or two were referred to along the way, but no issue was taken with the reference if they were. So he's not sought to go into these in detail with the witness for his explanation of them. So, again, the issue seems to us at the moment is one of authenticity, and perhaps you can tell us, Mr. Fila, if you challenge the authenticity of these. Now, the documents in question were those in the list from 1418 to 2166.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply don't know whether they're authentic or not. I have not seen anything to prove that they are. It wouldn't be fair on my part to say that they're not because I have no information to that effect. So the problem in principle is tendering documents through a witness who knows nothing about them, because the witness, too, is unable to say whether they're authentic or not. That's where the problem lies. I don't think the Prosecutor is a person who would purposely tender false documents; I don't think that for a moment. I have no such suspicions, but there are no grounds for me to believe either one or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, some -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is that there are no grounds to introduce the document through this witness because the witness cannot provide the grounds; that's the issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, some of these relate to the police. Those that do, are they -- is the authenticity of them challenged?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think we've already -- we already handled, I believe, P1992 yesterday -- Friday, and that was already denied admission. We also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I don't have 1992 on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. It wasn't on this list of this group of documents that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's confine ourselves to this section --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- of the documents that goes from 1418 to 2166 of the list that Mr. Petrovic identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From 1418 through --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe none of those are actually MUP documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's why I was moving on to the other section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The only document I think referred to specifically in the evidence to any extent of that group was 1967, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was some reference, I think, to 1460.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's the order of -- from the Supreme Command regarding subordination of the MUP, when the witness was talking about General Pavkovic had complained about that and General Ojdanic who had requested an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, apart from these various documents, reference was also made to 1468, which was a handwritten document, apparently notes from the meeting of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, it's the minutes of several meetings between July and October of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Handwritten?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's handwritten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that wasn't explored in evidence either, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. I only asked him about a couple of names to make an argument from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And 1898 which is Stevanovic's diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He was not asked about it. It's referred to in his written statement, but I didn't ask him any questions about it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is it referred to in the written statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll have to get the paragraph reference. Paragraph 72, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something very briefly with respect to the document mentioned by Mr. Hannis 4B, 1468, especially in relation to this document, there is no way that document can be admitted through this witness. The fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I'm sorry,, just let me complete what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Then Mr. Ivetic raised two documents 1249 and 1996. Now, 1249 you thought had been exhibited but wasn't, in fact. And 1996 was one which was intimated at a late stage. Now, again, Mr. Hannis, do you seek to have these admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, 1996 I do not intend to seek admitted at this time. I didn't ask this witness any questions about those. I'll have a written submission to make in connection with it later. And as to 1249, likewise, this was not shown to the witness. I may try to tender it later through another witness or with a written submission, but I'm not offering it at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will admit the following documents: 928, 929, 931, 932, 935, 938, and 941. There is now no objection to their admission, and we are satisfied that evidence demonstrates a basis for saying that they're authentic. Other documents which are not included in the list of documents to which Mr. Petrovic took exception at the outset of the evidence are admitted in the usual way, according to the use made of them in the course of the evidence. So far as the others, however, to which objection was taken are concerned, the Trial Chamber does not know enough about them at the moment to say that they should be admitted; however, there are signs in the submissions made by Mr. Hannis that a number of these documents, if not all of them, may well be admitted once the Trial Chamber is satisfied about the position, which it can't be at the moment. I say that because if counsel feel that if any of these documents are admitted they would have wanted to ask questions of this witness about them, then you should proceed to question the witness about them in case they are admitted, to the extent, that is, that you wish. However, where the issue for Defence counsel is explaining the content of the document and it's not felt necessary to do that through evidence, then that will be open to you to do in the form of response to any written submission the Prosecution will be required to make to support the admission to these documents. So, in other words you, will be able to advance any argument you wish in relation to the documents in due course before we make a decision on admitting them. But just in case that decision is to admit them and you think it necessary or helpful to ask this witness questions about them you should do so and make it clear to us at what stage in your cross-examination you're doing that so it's clear these questions are asked on the basis of the reservation of the admissibility of these various documents. Now, for the avoidance of any doubt, and please correct me if I make any mistakes on, this the documents to be admitted are: 1418, 1487, 1503, 2031, 2113, 2166, 1468 [sic], 1249. Now, remind me, Mr. Hannis, 1460 and 1967, did you say something about 1460?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, 1460 was discussed with the witness when we were talking about the issue of subordination of the MUP to the VJ. He was shown that document in connection with I believe it was 1459 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think in relation to 1460 and 1967, although they were referred to in the course of the evidence, the objection is to them being used on a stand-alone basis for reference in the course of the trial, not just in relation to matters explored with the witness. And since you want to use them for that purpose, then they will fall within the category of those to which you must make submissions before we decide the extent to which they are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These two documents are also included in that statement. 1898 I think falls into a different category, and the witness has referred to it specifically in his evidence. It, on the face of it, seems genuine to us. And to the extent that it has been explored in evidence, that one is admitted to -- if you wish to invite the Chamber again to explore the content of that without reference to any evidence about it, then again you would have to make a written submission to support that to which the Defence will have an opportunity to respond. But it's clearly admitted to the extent to which the witness referred to it in his evidence. Your submission, Mr. Hannis, should also deal with any exhibits from the Milosevic trial to make sure that they're cross-referenced adequately and it's clear to the Trial Chamber the extent to which you seek to have them admitted. Plainly, they're admitted to the extent to which they were used in the Milosevic trial. We may or may not give any weight to them. If you want to look at their contents is in some detail beyond the extent which they were referred to in the evidence, then, again, you would have to make a written submission explaining the basis on which you seek to do that, that is to establish their authenticity, essentially, and their relevance and probative value for the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is there any issue arising from that on which any counsel seeks clarification? Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe there is an omission in the transcript. Page 30, line 20, you gave a list of the collegium admitted into evidence, but P939 is missing. I may be wrong, but I see no reason for its admission. I think it should be on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're quite right and my attention's been drawn to that. For some reason, I don't have it listed as one that's been referred to, but you're telling me that Mr. Petrovic referred to that, do you? You see, one of the difficulties about this is it hasn't arisen by the Prosecution seeking to admit the documents; it's arisen by an objection being taken. So, Mr. Hannis, if there are others that weren't objected to and weren't referred to in the evidence, then there's no basis on which they'll be admitted because they're in the ether somewhere. But 939, since it falls within the sequence of the others, will also be admitted. Any other issue arising? Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. I seek clarification. I may have misunderstood, but I prefer to have this clarified. On page 31, lines 23 to 24, you list the documents that are to be admitted. From your previous decision, I understood -- I see document 1468 here. I understood that these documents would not be admitted. I wish it to be made clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I hope it's a mistake in the transcript and I didn't say that, but I certainly didn't mean to say it. These are documents on which submissions will be necessary before we determine whether they're admitted or not. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's how I understood it also, but unfortunately it was not reflected that way in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any other points? Very well. Mr. Fila, for you to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vasiljevic. My name is Toma Fila, and together with my colleague Mr. Petrovic, I appear for Nikola Sainovic. I will put, I hope, few questions, and later on you will see why I have to put questions at all. Please take your statement and look at paragraph 20. That's when you were waiting to be received by Mr. Milosevic; and because of something that was later shown on Belgrade television, I have to ask you: What did General Ojdanic say to you in connection with Pavkovic? What did he say he held against him when he saw Pavkovic coming out? You know what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And please then say -- tell me the same thing in relation to Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in relation to Pavkovic, he said he was surprised to see him there when he did not come to see him and was not informed about this by Milosevic. Also, he said that he knew that before that day when we were there together, he had arrived to visit Milosevic in Belgrade on more than one occasion. And he said that he knew that Pavkovic was providing better information to Mr. Sainovic than he was to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Later on you mentioned the names of two persons we will not mention for the sake of their families, who said that Pavkovic was seeing Sainovic. As far as I can understand, they did not attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do they know what Pavkovic discussed with Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The content of the conversation was not mentioned, merely the fact that he was coming there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that's all you know about this? Now I'll tell you why I'm putting these stupid questions to you. When you were answering Mr. Hannis's questions about this, journalists from the audience informed someone that you were saying that orders were being given by Sainovic to Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. I apologise for having asked you this. That's RTS, as you know, so I had to put that question to you. In relation to paragraphs 46 and 47 of your statement, you speak here about what you know about the Joint Command in 1998. Would you agree with me that your information about the Joint Command in 1998, when you were not holding that post, is a second-hand information which you received from Colonel Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have to slow down because we're speaking the same language, so we have to take the interpretation into account. In paragraph 46 of your statement, you speak about the coordination for joint operations, and there's one thing that remains unclear. Does this refer to 1999 or to 1998?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you put your question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What period does this refer to when you were in service or out of service?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the request?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, but your statement.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to what I know about 1999, that's one thing; and secondly, based on documents I saw dating from 1998, that's the meeting of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The inter-ministerial staff. The transcript mentions the staff, inter-ministerial is missing from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The next question I wish to put to you in that context is: As an experienced general, do you think it is necessary to have coordination between the Army of Yugoslavia and the MUP when operations are being carried out?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's normal, yes. But I draw a distinction between coordination and subordination and command. If they are jointly carrying out the same task, then there has to be coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But the chain of command remains?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I drew a distinction. When command is in question, that's a different question. That's not the same as coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you speak about coordination - and excuse me, but I was never a soldier, a good soldier anyway, so the questions may seem odd to you - but if I understood you correctly when you speak about coordination, it means that the chain of command remains intact?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's how it is in the case of coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well then. I understand you correctly. I now wish to have the document shown to you P1459 that we have been discussing so much, even though Mr. Hannis says it's 1460; in fact, it's 1459, that's Pavkovic's letter. Do you want me to give it to you this way or is it better for you to see it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's better for me to see it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You better take Mr. Hannis's copy because mine is all scribbled on.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, all right. If it's enlarged, I'll manage to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm interested in page 2.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Here, I've got it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I've noted 1460 as an order about subordination dated the 19th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and 1459 makes reference to it in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But 1459 was not one of the documents to which exception was taken; and, therefore, on the face of it, it's been admitted for the purpose for which it was used in the course of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I wanted to tell you, Your Honour, when you didn't want to hear me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what, are you objecting to its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. No, I wanted to talk about the numbers. No, I'm not objecting at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please pay attention to only this list part where it says "proposed measures." Now, there is this small debate among us about whether the translation is right or not, so I would like to ask you to read this whole sentence; what Pavkovic says exactly, the last bit, measures proposed.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to hear the objection again that I'm just a doll that's reading things out, a mannequin or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no. No, just read it out.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which sentence do you mean? "In accordance with the proclaimed state of war annul the order on their resubordination leave the command and commanding of the forces of the MUP" -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Slowly and from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the spirit of the constitution and existing laws and in accordance with the proclaimed state of war, either annul the order on their resubordination and leave the command and commanding of the forces of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia in the hands of the Ministry of the Interior as until now - staff of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia for Kosovo and Metohija through the Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Now we've heard it right. I just have one more question. Does that mean that this shows that the MUP is commanding the MUP forces in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As stated here, that's the way it's stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in one more thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I take it that the witness did not read the whole of that section, that he read from a certain point?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He read the part that I was interested in. You know, we don't want him to be a doll reading things out, just reading them out, just half the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did he know where to begin? I assume --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I told him. He has it in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You asked him to read from proposed measures, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, proposed measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, he didn't start reading -- he didn't start reading from there; he read from much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't want to offend him, so I shortened it so that he wouldn't have to read out the whole thing. I'm interested only in the part about the command and commanding the MUP forces of the Republic of Serbia as until now is conducted by the MUP on the basis that we conclude that the MUP commanded its troops. That is what I wanted to hear and that is what the witness confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm just trying to work out why the witness read not from where you asked him but from a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, later on I told him to start from this other place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You saw these measures that were proposed. I'm just interested in the following now. Was anything done in accordance with this request made by General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said, as can be seen from this document, that this is from the 25th of May. I know that General Ojdanic reacted towards President Milosevic, and I testified about that earlier. Now, when it was that he reacted, I cannot say now. I cannot say whether it was before or after this. As far as I know, it was before this, because what is mentioned here is the problem of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. So did something change in the situation on the ground; that's what I'd like to know?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say now. I don't think that anything changed in terms of the situation on the ground; however, the fact remains that -- well, this is practically a week after this particular date. On the 1st of June, I attended the meeting of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of June, I attended the meeting of the Joint Command in Pristina, where General Pavkovic was present and General Lazarevic, and I already described that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. All right. But that's a different matter. In relation to paragraph 47, I've already asked you -- yes, and you confirmed that this is the information given to you by Stojanovic. He did not present any particular details to you, Colonel Stojanovic, in this brief conversation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, this is the gist of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. And then he said to you that three civilians attended these meetings during the course of 1998?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Those were Minic, Sainovic, and Matkovic, as you said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You know that Minic was the president of the federal chamber and Sainovic -- rather, the assistant minister and Matkovic was the director of whatever and --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the document that I was shown, Matkovic is referred to as the vice-president of the SPS and the director --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm just asking you about your personal knowledge. What do you think, who is higher ranking, the vice-president of the Assembly or one of the five deputy prime ministers?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Assembly is the highest organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to hear. Now I'd like to read something else out to you. In the OTP, they showed you different statements from the Milosevic case. I don't want to show you all of this. I don't want to burden you with all of that, but I just want to tell you that in the Milosevic case Colonel Kotur testified. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You do. In order to check what I'm saying, the page is 4754, lines from 3 to 15 of the Milosevic transcript. He said that General Djakovic, who you mentioned a few moments ago that you know, said to him that Pavkovic said to him that meetings that were held with the members of the MUP that were attended by these civilians that you have just referred to, he should mark as meetings of the Joint Command because they didn't know what to call it. And certain numbers were given, and he says that that is what is stated in the letter of the Pristina Corps. Do you allow for that possibility, for that to be the case?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this would be a good time to take a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. We'll have to break now, Mr. Vasiljevic. The break on this occasion will be for half an hour, so if you could leave again with the usher we'll see you again at 11.15. And we shall resume then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were talking about this Joint Command. I would like to keep things as short as possible because you said that your knowledge was indirect. You saw documents. We've shown you many documents, or rather, you have been shown many documents of the Joint Command, this time and last time when you were in court. What we have to observe is that nowhere is there any mention of any commander of this Joint Command. There's no signature, no seal, no nothing. Did you see anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did on one document. There is a signature of General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But directly, since I am Defence counsel for Sainovic, I'm interested in civilians.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any signatures of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. We established together last time that there was this ledger of the Pristina Corps, so this command did not even have a ledger because Kotur spoke about those things, too. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any such thing. I don't know whether it exists, but I never saw any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. You said what it was that Colonel Stojanovic said to you, that there were three civilians in 1998. As far as I managed to understand what you were saying, Stojanovic did not speak about the actual persons who were on the Joint Command in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not 1998, he spoke about -- not 1999, he spoke about 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to hear. Now, again, I did not quite understand what you were saying yet again. In paragraph 49 of your statement, you say that the commander of the 3rd Army was in a sandwich between the Joint Command and his command, because in addition to his regular reports he had to submit reports to the Joint Command. You will agree with me that we never saw any written reports sent to the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were any written reports, but what I conveyed was my testimony from the meeting where I was, where General Pavkovic reported orally about the situation on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I'm really moving too fast. So what is written in paragraph 49 is your conclusion on the basis of that meeting, if I understand things correctly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the meeting and on the basis of what General Ojdanic said to me, that Pavkovic was reporting more --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. But these are not written reports. You're talking about things that were said at meetings, so oral reports.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't aware of how much I was hurrying, but I did not see any written reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, if we're talking about normal coordination, which is what you were talking about where you have representatives of the army and the MUP and they're agreeing on joint action, is it not a normal thing for both sides to present their positions, their views, if I can put it that way, to exchange views and exchange opinions. In your opinion what should this coordination be like?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that coordination should be distinguished from the system of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Objectively speaking, here there is an official name for this form of communication, that it is the Joint Command. They themselves accept that this was a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just the army, let it be clear.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not communicate with others outside the army. Now, in the war, since the forces of the MUP and all other forces are subordinated to the military, there -- no coordination was needed any longer. I've already said this. Since it was a state of war, it would have been far more efficient if a person either from the MUP or from anywhere, from the top echelons of the political sphere, would attend meetings of the staff of the Supreme Command like the Minister of Defence and General Velickovic to coordinate in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You're talking about Pavle Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1999. It was General ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
