utterances.text: If we do not challenge the fact that the police and the military had meetings on the ground down there, how could they be in this coordination except if they were saying things to each other?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one thing. If they're coordinating things, if these forces are not subordinated. But if these forces are subordinated then there is no further coordination; then the expression to be used is that tasks are assigned to the MUP or it is said in concerted action with. And also there is this other expression, resubordination of such and such a MUP unit to such and such a brigade and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. But you know from that letter - we're not going to talk about the authenticity of that letter, the one that you and I looked at a few moments ago - that resubordination was not actually carried out. If there is no resubordination, then it is only logical that there should be coordination; that's what you said a few moments ago, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But one week after this on the 1st of June, I attended something I was told was the Joint Command, so I attended this command.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, fine, let's not go into that.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is not an inter-ministerial staff. If this is an inter-ministerial staff, then this is the body that is in charge of the coordination. But the problem is if we have the command because then there is no coordination anymore but the chain of command, a system of issuing orders. I agree that this is quite illogical.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Fine. Also from the headings that I saw, I never saw any seals or stamps or I don't know where the seat was, the headquarters were. As far as I understood, it was a basement of some sort and some mail was received there for the Pristina Corps. Is that the fact?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not how I described it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No. No, please do go ahead?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not how I described it. I didn't say that this was a basement. It was an underground room. I said that this was a hall of some sort, maybe a cinema. I don't know what it was, in fact. But there were no seals, because everything was entered into the ledger of the Pristina Corps under the same reference number that was -- reference system that was common for all the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Fine. In that case, if I understand you correctly, you're saying that the chain of command of the Yugoslav army was intact from the top to the bottom?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- yes, it was intact. But in some of its segments, it was dysfunctional, so to speak. So the proposal to deploy forces, this is something that should be approved down the chain of command from the top down. Now, whether this was done in parallel to what was agreed at the meeting of the Joint Command and then daily reports were issued to the Supreme Command Staff, I don't know whether there was -- there were any breakdowns there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us now move on to something else. In paragraph 62 - and now let me move on to your notebook - these are excerpts from your diary P2592, and you mention Sainovic and his customs. Is this something that Sainovic came -- concluded after listening to Rade Markovic regarding the SAJ, because Rade Markovic was in charge of SAJ -- no, in fact, he was in charge of JSO.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the first to intervene before Mr. Sainovic, then it was General Pavkovic, then Rade Markovic made a few brief remarks. And we were talking about the paramilitary units, primarily the Skorpions and Jugoslav Petrusic, and then his comment followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to hear. Now let me move on to the meeting with Milosevic on the 17th of May. I've read all the statements that you made, the interviews, everything. When you talk about this meeting, as far as I was able to understand, this meeting at Milosevic's was preceded by a number of meetings that you talk about. General Ojdanic said he was very concerned about the situation and so on. I don't want to go into that. And then some preparations were made that would result in your departure for Kosovo. You speak about your impressions, the conversations that are apparently quite numerous. What I am bothered -- what bothers me, you talk about the good intentions by General Ojdanic, that they really wanted to investigate matters, but you see that these people are in the dock now. And the Prosecution contends that these people knew about all this and that these were some kind of comical, funny meetings where people didn't mean what they were saying. The indictment lists all these people --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and some other person we should not -- I have not yet asked my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I object to the characterisation of that question where he says that the Prosecution contends that these were some kind of comical, funny meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's what I'm saying. This was not interpreted correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So could we then conclude -- were you able to conclude that these people really wanted to solve those things, to punish those people for those crimes? You were all serious people, generals. We can see what you were saying. This is what I want to hear. Was this a serious meeting where serious conclusions were being made and serious analysis were being made. This is what I want to know. What is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What meeting do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: 17th of May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Vasiljevic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was my point what meeting were you talking about, because the question said prior to this 17th of May meeting there were a number of meetings and then the question was: Were these people serious? Which people and which meeting? I understand the reference to General Ojdanic, but now he's extending it to everybody who was in every meeting. We need some precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, can we be clear about which meeting and which personnel you're talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about this whole series of events where General Dimitrijevic was participating with General Pavkovic and all the others that preceded the 17th of May meeting and the and the meeting of the 17th of May 1999, which is the end of this series of events. I do have to apologise, General Vasiljevic, I said Dimitrijevic and I meant Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I meant the participants, some or all of them, you, for instance, did you take your job serious? Were all these meetings serious and in particular the one on the 17th of May?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you a collective assessment of all the meetings. I can talk about the meeting that took place on the 13th of May when I was a participant. It was a meeting at General Ojdanic's. I can tell you about the preparations for the 16th of May meeting where a report was made by General Pavkovic. I can talk about the General Staff personnel at the meeting of the 17th of May, and I can say that these were very serious meetings, that a lot of effort was put to prepare the material for these meetings. And I have already mentioned in my evidence the main topic discussed were the war crimes; and then I said that Milosevic skipped the most important almost, and that was the proposal by Pavkovic and by General Ojdanic to establish an independent state commission that would go to Kosovo and check the situation. He switched the premises and he did not want to discuss that. He discussed other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So your conclusion is that the General Staff took its job seriously and conscientiously?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At that meeting, according to your notes, Sainovic makes the following proposal, that's the 17th of May: That an independent supervisor be sent; and from your notebook, I can only conclude that Sainovic was not the supervisor. But I failed to comprehend what -- what was the point in that? What was your interpretation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not interpreting things; I merely made notes that I was able to make. Since a proposal was made by General Pavkovic, who intervened in the discussion before Sainovic, about the necessity to establish an independent state commission for Kosovo, Mr. Sainovic agreed with that but he did not term it state commission. He used the term supervisor, a supervisory body, not himself, but somebody else who would go to Kosovo and who would have the political weight, the authority, to ensure that an independent inquiry is made into these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 68, you quote Milosevic, what he said, about the problems between MUP and the Yugoslav army. He made certain suggestions as to how this should be resolved. You know what I'm talking about. Am I right when I conclude that the problems emerging between the MUP and the Yugoslav army, that they were actually resolved in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in -- this is not something that can be concluded in the context of your question. His stressing of the alleged number of problems which led him to ask for an urgent meeting between the Yugoslav army and the MUP, the essence was not in the seriousness of the problems or in the necessity for him to deal with them. What he actually did is he switched the premises. He skipped the war crimes, reducing this to an issue that involves Boca Medic and the greater Serb advocates. But the problem that the Yugoslav army presented - and this is something that Mr. Sainovic agreed to at this meeting - he simply skipped this whole item and this was never done. Myself and Gajic did not go down there as a commission or as supervisor. We were tasked by General Ojdanic to deal with strictly military issues, to talk to security organs, and also to gain some more information about the war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But this was done bona fide, you did not simply pose there. You wanted to really do the job?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would like you to look at paragraph 72, the Prosecutor did not ask you any questions about that, and this is something that was entered into evidence. We're talking about General Obrad Stevanovic. We can conclude that you never saw and you never attended this meeting until the Prosecutor showed you those papers.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what you're saying is based on the assumption that what you were given was authentic, that these -- that this really was a notebook owned by General Obrad Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given this as a document that was already used in trial, and I did follow the Slobodan Milosevic trial while it was broadcast. I followed the testimony by Mr. Stevanovic for the good part. The part that was not in the transcript during his testimony, is something that I would like to comment now. The claims that I made, there are no corpse, no crime, we should do this quickly, before that, during the trial, Stevanovic was asked: What does it mean that the military service was supposed to do something underhand? I'm paraphrasing things now. And his reply was -- in fact, changed the essence. He said that the Siptar terrorist forces learned or decided that bodies should be removed because no body, no crime; and then when the UN mission arrives, the bodies should be brought back and -- to be used for these purposes. And this was something that was provided, this data were provided by the military service. The military service never did that. I think that this was a fabrication, and this is the context in which I was shown the notebooks, the notebook. Now it is for others to decide whether it is authentic or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I am interested in is when you look at the notebook, there's only one date there, and that's the 7th of May. And the next date is the 20 something or other -- the 20th of May, and that's after the text that we're talking about. And now on this page that you looked at, where the elements that you just commented are, there are interruptions or blank areas, and then after one of those blank areas you can see Saja. What I want to know is whether you can claim that Saja was there at the meeting and whether he really said that.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I cannot claim that. I did not see the whole notebook in order to be able to give you an answer. I was just shown this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, this concludes my cross-examination on the notebook. Thank you very much. Now I have to ask you something that might look strange to you. I have to apologise for asking you stupid questions once again. Did anyone change the report that you submitted to Ojdanic, the report from Kosovo? For instance, Sainovic; Sainovic says: No. No, this cannot be like that. Let's put it like this.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody altered my reports, not in the chain of command and least of all could it have been done by Sainovic, who I did not have any contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, Tanic talked about that. In paragraph 78 of your statement, you talk about meeting that Pavkovic later on termed the Joint Command meeting. I didn't quite understand you. What did you mean when you say "later?"

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I arrived at the premises -- this was some kind of a military headquarters, so it was a command or a forward command post, and then he said to me there would be a meeting of the joint staff there and the people present there would attend. I think that he invited me in order to meet some of these people. I had known General Lukic from MUP, and that is when the term was used. But I have to apologise. And Colonel Stojanovic told me when we headed there, that that would be the meeting of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now you say that the representatives of the state security division was not present there. Do you think that this representative should have been there? Was it that -- was that because the SAJ was there in the field? Why was -- should he have been present, and why was he not there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not make any remarks to that effect. I didn't even know whether this person was a part of that body. I mentioned one person who was supposed to be there, who wasn't there. And the reason was provided why he wasn't there, but there was no discussion at all about Mr. Gajic. Now, as to why he was supposed to be there, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One thing I should have clarified before -- one thing I should have clarified before we moved on to this. The meeting that you attended on the 17th of May, did General Stevanovic attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're talking about the 17th of May meeting at President Milosevic's, nobody from MUP, from the public security division was not present there. The minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic was not there, Djordjevic was not there, Stevanovic, General Lukic, they were not present there. Now, as for the state security division, only Rade Markovic was represented -- was there. If you mean the meeting of the Joint Command on the 1st of June, where I was present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, this one of the 17th of May, and just to clarify one other thing. Stevanovic was at that stage an assistant minister. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was he then in charge of the state security and, therefore, superior to Markovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. So which assistant minister was responsible for state security at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The minister is in charge of the state security division, and then there is a chief of the state security division and General Djordjevic. These are two separate divisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Markovic was the chief of the state security division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. What I'm trying to establish is who was his political superior, and are you saying that that was Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Formally, Rade Markovic's superior was Stojiljkovic, the Minister of the Interior; but in fact, it was President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were -- Stojiljkovic was the Minister of the Interior. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There were assistant ministers of the interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did one of them have responsibility for state security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Rade Markovic. His title, whether it was assistant minister, I don't know, but in essence that's what he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So he did not hold his post as a person employed in the service; he was a politician holding the post of assistant minister. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I want to say is that even before the chief of the state security division, ever since the 1990s, the person to hold that position was selected very carefully, because this was the most sensitive division, the Ministry of the Interior, and it was Milosevic himself who made that decision. In 1998, or rather, in 1997, the Minister of the Interior of Serbia was replaced. He asked for a briefing from the chief of the state security division on issues he was dealing with. I testified about that previously, and they expressed their satisfaction and they addressed Milosevic directly. They said they did not want to be subordinated to the ministry of Serbia, and for this reason a document was issued transferring the competency so that the president of Yugoslavia could have direct contacts with the State Security Service. So that within the framework of the Ministry of the Interior, the state security division was far more independent than other sectors and they were directly linked to Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the diary entry made by Stevanovic for the 17th of May, does he refer to Markovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether Markovic is referred to, but if he is then it can only be that Markovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, but what I'm trying to do is establish whether there's any connection between the diary entry and the fact that Sainovic and Markovic remained behind in his office after the meeting that you attended concluded on the 17th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you're saying that Stevanovic had no link to the work of the security service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't Stevanovic. I don't know whether it's written wrongly somewhere. After the meeting of the 17th of May, when the military persons left, Rade Markovic was called back by Milosevic and he remained with Mr. Sainovic and Markovic. I didn't mention Stevanovic at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know that. What I'm trying to establish is whether there might be a link between that situation and the notes made by Stevanovic; in other words, whether he may have arrived into that situation or not. That's all. But you're telling me that there would be no reason for that because he's got no connection with the security service. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're using the generic term security service, instead of public security versus state security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, state security. I am sorry. State security service. And you tell me that Stevanovic had no responsibilities for state security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At one point you mention that Pavkovic said to you that the meeting would also be attended by Sainovic, but as far as I was able to understand he did not mention Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall saying that Pavkovic said Sainovic would be at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you're certain he didn't say that about Andjelkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, he said nothing about either of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, you say when they arrived at the meeting, you were already there, all the rest of you, and the officers stood up. They all stood up when the deputy prime minister of the federal government walked in. Is it normal, is it good manners in the country we come from for people to rise to their feet when the deputy prime minister enters; or is that something unusual? Do we have any kind of good manners? Would you explain that a little bit.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first, I didn't say it was only the officers who rose to their feet; we all did. If you're talking about MUP officers, you're right, but it was actually all of us. Well, it's well-known what Mr. Sainovic's post was, and on any other occasion - I'm not referring just to the Joint Command - but when the chairperson or the most senior person enters a meeting, it's normal for everybody to rise to their feet. I didn't see it that way, that we were rising to our feet only for the deputy prime minister. We would have risen to our feet for any chairperson.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you said he was treated with respect by all those present. Is it unusual for a deputy prime minister to be treated with respect?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you keep mentioning the deputy prime minister of the federal government. I never gave him that title. I spoke about Mr. Sainovic, and you are mentioning his post. At that time, I wasn't actually thinking about: Oh, yes, here comes the deputy prime minister. He was a person who had dignity, who had authority. He was a high-ranking politician in Belgrade, and because we had respect for him we rose to our feet. I wouldn't link this up with any other contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So was it something quite normal?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was normal for us to rise to our feet when anybody presiding over a meeting entered the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In paragraph 80, you are saying who Sainovic represented. Would you allow the possibility that he was representing the federal government there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot exclude the possibility. I observed that when Mr. Sainovic is mentioned, in brackets it's usually mentioned whether he's representing the MUP or the Army of Yugoslavia or someone else. So it's enough to say "Sainovic," and everybody knew what post he held, both in the federal government and here in this staff or this command. And you will come to your own conclusions about that, but it was enough in that body to say "Sainovic." Everybody knew who he was. I crossed it out in the statement but it's still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You are saying that it was about the daily situation in Kosovo, that various people spoke. This lasted some 20 minutes, and then everybody had a drink. Now, sir, it's well-known that it's normal in our part of the world to offer people food and drink, but in serious meetings this is not done. Was this a visit by Sainovic to the people at that meeting? And that's why there were drinks and dinner, because all that was lacking was music for this to be transformed into a different kind of gathering. The people in white you mention were waiters after all, because this was in a hotel, Hotel Grand?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what the situation was quite objectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, I missed the reference to people in white, was that in an earlier question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] White shirts. It's in the statement. It says that soldiers wearing white shirts served drinks; it's in Mr. Vasiljevic's statement. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not white shirts, white coats.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, it says "shirts" here.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I go on? I attended many serious meetings; and when the meeting was over, there would be lunch or dinner. So this was just a normal soldiers' dinner, such as was usual. It was the same kind of food that was usually served; it wasn't anything special. And these were not waiters from The Grand Hotel. I'm not even sure it was in the Grand Hotel. In the commands, there were soldiers designated to serve at table; and for reasons of hygiene, they would wear white coats. I attended a working meeting. I concluded that this was the briefing for that day by people from the MUP and from the army, and there was a brief discussion of what was to happen the next day, the action towards Drenica, Trpezarci with 300 policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise. In the statement it says "in white coats" -- rather, it says "in white shirts." Had it said "in white coats," I would have been able to understand because I served in the army and I know what this looked like. You said that at this working meeting nobody was in command, no orders were issued, nobody stood up and said: I order this, I order that. There was a working atmosphere. My question is now the following. You say that your impression was that these meetings were held on a daily basis. Can you conclude that Sainovic was able to be present every day, because you saw him in Belgrade so he couldn't have been.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that he was there every day. I'm just saying that my impression on the basis of the briefings which related to activities of the previous day was that these meetings were held on a daily basis. I'm not saying that Mr. Sainovic chaired those meetings on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Those were all my questions. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 5 of your statement, you say that after the NATO attack in March 1999 you felt it was your patriotic duty offer your services. Can you tell us what the general mood was in the country as regards the NATO attacks on Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that there was a widespread feeling of patriotism. Regardless of the fact that it was the strongest force in the world attacking a small country, morale was exceptionally high and people were determined to defend the country. In this difficult situation, rallies of support to the army and the MUP were organised in Belgrade. So I can only describe the situation in the most positive terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Would I be right, General, in saying that the vast majority, if not all, retired officers offered their services to the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that's correct. Objectively, every man who was re-activated and assigned war duty felt this to be an honour. In relation to the security organs, I can say that almost all the retired officers of the service addressed me, came to me, asking what they could do to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let's go back. But, first of all, was it the constitutional duty of every citizen, especially a trained soldier, to participate in the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We'll now move on to paragraph 11 of your statement, in which you speak about the daily meetings held at the Supreme Command Staff. In your statement, you say that representatives of the security administration always attended those meetings. Bearing in mind your general information and your replies to Mr. Hannis, I'm asking you now in general: Had there been a plan to expel the Albanian population and had the General Staff of the army or the Supreme Command Staff planned and executed or in any way supported this, would these daily meetings in the Supreme Command Staff have been a place where such plans should have been discussed, developed, or elaborated in any way?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state categorically that there was no such plan. There was absolutely no such plan. What the situation on the ground was, that's a separate story, but there was no plan. Had there been a plan, then the effects, the results, would have been monitored and would have been included in the briefings. Certainly there would have been responsibilities in relation to that plan, but nothing like that was discussed or could have been discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Were minutes of these meetings taken or - to put it differently - to the best of your knowledge should minutes have been taken at such Supreme Command Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I did not attend these meetings, I cannot say whether or not minutes were taken, but I'm convinced they were because that would have been normal. It would have been obligatory, and the daily operative report of the staff of the Supreme Command would have been based on these.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now that we are referring to reports, is it correct that in the operative duty team of the Supreme Command Staff, the president [as interpreted] of the security administration was always present?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And the responsibility of this person, was it to study the point in the report referring to security and, based on that, that point in the other reports would be done?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was the duty from the staff sector I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, 64, 21, it says "president," instead of "representative of the security administration."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to the interpreters. I will try to move slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In this report that was compiled by the Supreme Command Staff, the combat report of the Supreme Command Staff, there was a particular item related to security. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we talk about combat reports, am I right, General, if I say that a combat report is a basic combat document from which information should be gathered on the situation in subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only to gather information in that way, that is just one method. On the basis of combat reports, to have insight as to the situation in the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that point of view, you are right; however, in addition to that, in addition to that combat report, daily combat report that comes in, the commander also has other methods made available to him, to call people in for briefings, as he called us, from security, then also to send teams out into the field as was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we are going to get to that. I am following your statement. You elaborated that in your statement, so we will get to that. But now that we are discussing the combat report, am I right that the -- or at combat report is a basis for the command to pass possible new discussions or take measures on the basis of the reports received?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because actually that describes the daily situation on the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you to look at 3D480.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 3D480 is the document I'm talking about, and you will see that it is the same document as P1475. The Prosecutor proffered only one part of this document, and we want to tender it in its entirety. I don't want to have any confusion, and that's why I'm referring to the Prosecution number as well; however, in the Defence we are referring to the document in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We are looking now at the document from the 2nd of April, 1999, that speaks of an order and it refers to instructions to the armed forces of Yugoslavia on the implementation of international humanitarian law. I want to say that the second page of this document, rather, paragraph 8, that is the one that I would like to see on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please see paragraph 8. The English version as well, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, so that you would not read it, I am going to read out paragraph 8 which says: "Against any member of the Yugoslav army who fails to adhere to this order, undertake measures of criminal responsibility about which the Supreme Command shall be informed through combat reports." My question, General: Paragraph 8 of this order, does it not reflect what a combat report should include inter alia? So extraordinary circumstances which would include certain measures of criminal responsibility, rather, criminal prosecution against perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm right, the way I read this paragraph, paragraph 8, you said that the Supreme Command should be informed; whereas, I am referring to it in a continuous tense here, not only once but several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I don't know if you can see it right, whether you have a very legible copy --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there is this highlight here, so I cannot see it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'll get you a copy.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the essence is the same. There is nothing to be contested here. This is the obligation that existed. And when I was re-activated and when I assumed my duty on the 27th of April, 1999, immediately in addition to the equipment that was issued to me, I was given a brochure containing a compilation of regulations in reference to the Geneva Conventions. So this is fully in line with this order of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'm going to show you another document P1744 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, can we have this document here for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The document is signed by the Chief of Staff, General Dragoljub Ojdanic; however, General, could you explain to us the stamp on the right, the right half of this document if I can put it that way. And, possibly, if you could explain what the handwritten notes in the lower right-hand corner denote.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the right half of this page, there is a stamp from the teleprinter station, and it shows the number and how this order was dispatched as a dispatch that went to the command. Underneath, in hand, the commands are written out, the commands of the different units to which this was sent, that is to say the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Army, and not to read the whole thing, the air force and the air defence, the navy, and so on. So that shows who this was submitted to. This last bit PKM, that is rear command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And the numbers are probably the time references to the time when this was sent to them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when it was originally dispatched.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1744, could I see that now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Again, it's a document of the Supreme Command Staff which pertains to reporting. The 15th of April, 1999, is the date. If you look at this document in its entirety, I'm not going to read any particular parts of it --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could it please be enlarged a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We're going to provide you with a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, if you look at this document in its entirety, am I right if I say that this is one of the documents through which the defence of the -- the staff of the Supreme Command is trying to improve reporting by subordinate units, wanting it to be timely, in view of the fact that in the chain of reporting there was -- there were, rather, certain interruptions due to the fact that many things were taking place in the field?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 18, General, you talked about control as one of the possibilities to find out what was going on in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please see document 3D489 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It's a document dated the 20th of April, 1999, again a document of the Supreme Command Staff. General, in the heading it says: "Tour of inspection of units and providing them with professional assistance." Is this the same type of control or supervision that you and Gajic were conducting when sent by General Ojdanic after the meeting of the 17th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is in terms of the arms and services. A team was sent. Our team was sent along the lines of the security administration. We also had a short written order concerning an official mission, official travel. Such an order is always written in cases of official travel, what you're travelling for and what is to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When returning from the field, these teams submitted reports, as stated in the last paragraph of this document. On the 20th of April, 1999, for this particular case that this document refers to. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to see 3D481 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It is yet another control. It's a document of the Supreme Command Staff of the 8th of May, 1999, with practically identical content, general content. Again, this is touring the units and giving them professional assistance. This document, General, does it reflect a similar situation, like the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, it's a mistake. I'm sorry. It should be 3D491.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me try to find it as well, if I can. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem on e-court now. I think it's all right now, that we have the right document on e-court, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, just a brief question. Does this document reflect the same situation like the previous one?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, like 3D489.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what you talked about in paragraph 18 of your statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please move into closed session for a moment, because I'm going to ask the witness a few details about paragraph 20. [In English] Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did we hear evidence in private session in relation to this earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, very well. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, when you were invited to the meeting -- to meet with Mr. Milosevic because of the contact you had with the person whose name again we mentioned in private session, is it true that General Ojdanic supported you in a situation where there was a risk that you may come under flak because of unauthorised contacts with that person? I don't know if I'm describing this situation correctly.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question. Objectively speaking, I have to say that I really respect the fact that when Mr. Milosevic made this remark about me, that even before I was able to respond General Ojdanic said that I had done what I had done on his orders. And my life experience has taught me that this is not always the case, that the superiors do not always explain the acts of their subordinates. And he really acted as an officer and a as human being should.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Knowing General Ojdanic as much as you do on the basis of your work with him and on the basis of what you've just told us, would he be the man who would push his subordinates forward in order to hide behind them and to protect himself by shifting the blame on to them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of my knowledge of General Ojdanic, he's not that kind of a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now let me move on to paragraph 22 of your statement. In this part of your statement, you speak about territorial units and military districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like document P1471 to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you know that immediately after the war broke out on the 31st of March, 1999, the Supreme Command Staff issued an order establishing the territorial military detachment that would be staffed by conscripts of Albanian and other ethnic origins living in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I was re-activated, I did not come across this document so I'm not familiar with it. Its date is almost one month earlier than the date of my re-activation. But this document speaks about the need to include in territorial detachments the Siptar or the Albanian population and all the other ethnicities living in Kosovo. I remember that I was quite taken aback by a situation that I encountered when I visited the security organs in Kosovo. I think this was the security organ in the Prizren military sector, and his name I think was Milivoje Milisavljevic, and he briefed us on the composition. He had three military territorial detachments; and when he briefed us on the procedure, about the composition of the detachment, out of almost 2.300 people in those units, 650 of them were Muslims, or rather, Albanians or Goranis; about a hundred were Muslims; there were 15 Turks; and one Albanian; and one Macedonian. I found it quite interesting at the time, and this is why I recall this, the figures. I don't know whether this was done in accordance with this order, but the fact remains that in this very small unit we did not have a mono-ethnic composition. I don't know about this order, but I do know about the actual situation in the three territorial detachments, which means that they probably obeyed this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if you look at paragraph 6 in this order, "Appoint professional servicemen of Siptar ethnicity to command positions, as per wartime establishment." General, in the security administration, did you have any professional officers of Albanian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1999 when I got there, there were no such people in the security administration. But I do believe that perhaps in the Pristina Corps, I knew an Albanian that continued to serve even after 1992/1993. Now, as to whether he was in service later on, I don't know. I didn't meet him or anything, but there were Albanians serving in the Yugoslav army. I know that that was the case in Novi Pazar. In the brigade there, there was a man of Albanian ethnicity, but I have to admit that this was a rarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, the previous answer with numbers in it, does that relate to 1999? It must do I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The way I understood the witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, this is exactly the situation that Mr. Petrovic was critical of. I see you're taking no exception to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not at the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document also pertains to the evidence by Colonel Pesic on pages 7169 through 7170 and 7250 in the transcript in this case. And now I would like the witness to be shown document P1479.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Vasiljevic, in paragraph 26 of your statement, you talk about certain orders that related to volunteers. And I would like to go through some of those and then I will be asking you some additional questions in this respect. So this is P1479. It's an order by the Supreme Command Staff dated the 7th of April, 1999. If you look at paragraph 1 in this order, it talks about the reception centres that should be established as temporary facilities or temporary compositions. Could you tell us, what does it mean, General Vasiljevic, temporary composition or unit?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A temporary unit is the unit that is established ad hoc, on an ad hoc basis, to tackle a specific situation that arises. The reasons why such units are established can vary. In this specific case if we're talking about the reception of the volunteers, in my opinion, it gives a certain political weight. Essentially, it's a political issue rather than a military question, a military fact. The military was strong enough. Objectively speaking, the situation would not have a different outcome without the volunteers, but the volunteers showed that the whole people was ready to join in the war, the fight. On the basis of this document, this is a document from the beginning of April, specifies quite stringent criteria for the admission of volunteers. And, if I may, I would like to give you an answer as to the question whether the same criteria applied to the admission into the MUP ranks. I think that the criteria were absolutely the same. The health, good health, not as -- the person should not have been assigned to any other formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to go through this order in quite some detail. So paragraph 1, the reception centre, the command of the 3rd Army had its reception centre in Nis, while the 1st Army had its reception centre in Belgrade. Does this correspond to what you knew?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the reception centre was not in Bubanj Potok. At the time when this order was written, it was probably there. But when I was re-activated, it was located in Grocka and Bubanj Potok had already been targeted and was already destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to another document showing precisely that. In paragraph 3 of this document, we see a list of the elements that should be established before a volunteer is admitted to the Yugoslav army. We're still on page 1 of the English text, and here we have a whole series, or rather, six items that should be checked in the triage of the volunteers. General, is this what should be done by any command acting conscientiously in order to avoid any problems and to induct or conscript people who are -- who might cause any problems?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I actually did provide this information. I don't know whether it was in my evidence in this trial or in the previous trial. We received 5.000 applications by volunteers, and 2.500 of them passed, so 50 percent failed and were not admitted as volunteers in the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to move on to page 3 of the English version, that's paragraph 8. General, it says here: "When assigning volunteers to VJ commands, units, and installations, it is prohibited to group them within one unit," and then the reasons are provided for this kind of stipulation. This prohibition of putting them all into groups, into one group, was this some kind of a preventative measure to prevent any problems that might arise if a group of people of the same criminal mindset attempt to infiltrate the system, such as the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I have to perhaps give you an additional explanation here. When it says here: "Given earlier negative experiences," I think that the experience referred to is not the experience between the 23rd of March and the 7th of April. This refers to the negative experience in the earlier period, so 1991/1992, but at that time the volunteer issue was resolved in a completely different way. Certain parties, political parties, in fact, gathered those volunteers and they did not apply any criteria that would judge their worth, but on the basis of their political affiliation. When I was in the army, at that time we had great problems with the volunteers, and I mentioned the accommodation centre, the reception centre, in Sremska Palanka, where those volunteers created an incident because they refused to remove their parting insignia. So this is a reference to the negative experience from the previous period, not the very beginning of the war here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 10 prohibits the admission as volunteers to the VJ commands, units, and installations of members of paramilitary groups and individuals already present in the zones of responsibility without the prior completion of the procedures described in this order.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this paragraph, again, has a preventative character. It does not reflect the situation in the field. As far as I know, the paramilitary formations in the classic sense of the word did not exist. What we had were groups that got together, and they acted together as part of those units that had already gone through the reception centres. But the problem was that the order of the Supreme Command Staff was not complied with in some of the units. This was not the general situation, prevalent situation. But, for instance, in the 37th Brigade in Glogovac, there was such a group and it did have negative consequences. The order, however, was clear enough that the group should not be admitted as such but people in accordance with their wartime assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now let us look at the last sentence here where it says this order precedes other orders and two orders are listed here. You can see before the 7th of April the General Staff of the VJ issued orders relating to the admission of the volunteers. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This order was signed by the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, General Dragoljub Ojdanic. And now, General, on the next page, again, we have the stamp and some handwritten notes. Do these handwritten notes describe the same situation that you explained to us in the first document that I showed you, and that was 3D480. So we have the reception and the dispatching stamp and the units listed here.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it is quite interesting here that we have here a KVOBGD, that is the Belgrade Military District Command -- Belgrade Military Sector Command, and this was a very small sector, in fact. But because this reception centre was subordinate to the 1st Military District that was located in Belgrade, then in order to make things easier, to speed things up, I can see that this was sent directly to the Belgrade Military Sector Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me -- we didn't go through this. But in paragraph 5, it is stated that a group of officers is actually placing its -- they are placing themselves to the military sector in Belgrade for the execution of this task, and that might be the reason why this was sent directly also to the Belgrade military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have been told by my colleagues that this might be an appropriate time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Vasiljevic, we'll be breaking again, this time for lunch, we'll be breaking for an hour, so can you please return at quarter to 2.00. You can now leave with the usher. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall sit again at quarter to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown in e-court document 3D481.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is another document of the Supreme Command Staff dated the 14th of April, 1992. It's an order on the treatment of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The year is 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And it repeats to a large extent the order of the 7th of April, 1999; however, some additional measures are introduced. So please look at item 1, the paragraph before the last, which says that psychological examination of the volunteers should be carried out, they should be provided with weapons, and equipment registered in the records. And if we look at the paragraph above, it says, "Make sure to engage a sufficient number of security organs, a military police detachment, and psychologists at the reception centres." Unlike the previous order, we have an additional preventive measure, that is psychological processing, as it says here. Do you have any comment on this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was re-activated, which was on the 27th of April, we already had a security organ in the Grocka reception centre and expert assistance was being provided. It was General Gajic who inspected their work. On that occasion, we discovered an omission in that centre where the procedure was bypassed when a self-styled captain of the military police was received. After a detailed check, it was established that he was neither a reserve officer nor a member of the military police at any time, so he was removed from the centre. And I do know that the security organ monitored the work of the reception centre. As for psychological processing, in the previous order, you can see that a psychological and psychiatric evaluation is required.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same item, it says that volunteers should be once more told that when they put on a uniform they become members of the army and that after that any -- anyone leaving the unit would be a deserter. General, does this mean that an attempt was being made to eliminate any group of so-called weekend warriors or adventurers or persons who considered the war to be some sort of personal adventure of their own?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this element here was introduced based on the negative experiences of 1991. There was so-called weekend warriors, who turned up in the army when they felt like it and left whenever they wanted to. To the best of my knowledge, this was not the practice when we were at Kosovo, Gajic and I. But I don't exclude the possibility that some individual cases may have occurred and that that's why this was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The next paragraph, which is page 2 in the English text and also page 2 in Serbian, bans or prohibits the reception of volunteers and it repeats members of paramilitary units and so on. You already commented on this.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: However, I wish to draw your attention to item 2.2, which says that: "Conscripts who have not completed their military service should not be admitted as volunteers." You will see this here "do not admit as volunteers any recruits," and so on.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, this also referred to people who arrived as volunteers or were received in the reserve MUP forces; and in general, those who for whatever reason whatsoever, either because they were not old enough or because they had health problems and were declared unfit for military service, should now be received as volunteers. Only those young men or people who did not have a wartime assignment could be received as volunteers. And this could also apply to those who had done their military service but for health reasons were declared unfit for military service. So these are the persons being referred to and also persons younger than 18 or 19. I have seen orders more than once. I think this is the third document I've seen which shows that special care was taken concerning the volunteers being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, this is a question to try to clarify what might otherwise become confusion in my mind. I understood that once a man had done his military service, he was still registered at the military district as a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that's right, who could have possibly ever become a volunteer if you had to have completed military service to qualify as a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's ask the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you answer that, Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. You are quite right. On completing one's military service, one was entered into the military register at the military district. Some persons, because there was no need, were not assigned from that list to wartime units as reservists. Volunteers could be those who had completed their military training and done their military service, but for whatever reason were not given a wartime assignment to a wartime unit. That's one category of persons. Please let me finish. The second category, although they did have a wartime assignment in a wartime unit, but according to the wartime plan the unit had not been activated, that person also could apply as a volunteer. These are the two categories of persons who could be admitted as volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So by the -- is this the 14th of April? You're saying that not every able-bodied citizen had been mobilised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There were such cases because if his wartime unit had not been activated according to the war plan, he was practically at liberty, but he could volunteer. And there was some wartime units that were not activated according to the plan because they were not located in the area where the military operations were going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I'll ask you about another category of persons. In item 3 of this order, volunteers are mentioned who are foreign citizens, foreign nationals, and a training battalion was provided for their training. Am I right in saying that any foreign national had to undergo military training?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and my security organs had no contact with such persons because in view of the date of this order, mid-April, they had already been admitted. I know that there were certain foreign nationals who volunteered, and I was briefed about them and I knew that they behaved properly. I cannot tell you what the exact procedure was for their admission -- admittance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just draw your attention to the last paragraph of this item and the last sentence which says: "During the training of volunteers, specifically warn them that unlawful and other negative behaviour will not be tolerated," and then it brackets "theft, looting, torching, smuggling, et cetera," and that "legal measures applicable in wartime will be taken against the perpetrators of such acts."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you expect me to comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, if you can. This was also included in the previous order.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have already commented on this. This was a general warning, the kind of warning I myself was given when I was re-activated. So this is something that the volunteers in the army were also given.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In item 4, volunteers are again prohibited from being grouped in special units; and if we look at page 4 in the English, a single collection centre is designated for all volunteers who were foreign nationals. This was the one in Grocka. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said, when I was re-activated I didn't have any contacts with them, but the order did regulate this and they were admitted in Grocka. When General Gajic visited the centre, I did not hear from him that there were any strange -- foreigners there. They'd already been through the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the same order - and we're still on item 6, page 4 in the Serbian text and it's the page we see on the monitor in English - the last sentence says for the needs of the work -- the requisite number of psychologists and psychiatrists will be designated, and this was so that one of the elements of this order could be implemented.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a complex order, so this refers to the item concerning psychological training and a special organ is being designated here to implement that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, would I be right in saying that by these few orders that we have been through, the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia constantly kept improving the procedure for admitting volunteers in an effort to avoid negative consequences?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a conclusion one can draw from these orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P11943 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is a letter from the Supreme Command Staff dated the 20th of April, 1999, concerning the problems of assigning volunteers to the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Could we have that number again. On my screen that's 11943, and that's -- we haven't gotten that far yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope we won't get there. It's 1943.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is a letter sent by the Supreme Command Staff, and it's dated the 20th of April, 1999. And it mentions certain omissions which caused part of the problems, and the General Staff has taken steps to rectify the situation. General, when we look at this document, we see that the reception centre sent back a certain number of persons who did not get through the screening, and that they were received in the reception centre of the 1st Army. You've already testified about this. It's also evident from this document that some volunteers were sent back from the Pristina Corps and that some of them were being prosecuted. My question is: Does this document show that the general -- that the Supreme Command Staff reacted on time, in a timely manner, to these negative events and that the 3rd Army responded in time, reacted in time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, please. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My objection, Your Honour, this is for summation. I don't think it's appropriate for this witness to give his opinion. The document speaks for itself to a certain extent. This is the sort of in the nature of the complaint I had from Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's exactly the complaint you had from Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Visnjic, what do you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me ask the General whether he had seen this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it now. I haven't seen it before, but it is in accordance with everything I said beforehand and everything that was displayed through the previous documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, I'm going to ask you about this particular document now. On page 1 in the Serbian text which is page 2 in the English language.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 2 of the English on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It is stated in the third paragraph in English and the last paragraph in Serbian it says: "A number of volunteers of around 50 percent subsequently gave up their deployment and engagement in the war units of the Army of Yugoslavia stating that they were not you willing to obey the rules unreservedly." General, this number, 50 percent, does it correspond to what you told us that roughly out of 5.000 volunteers only two and a half thousand managed to get through the screening?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The objection still stands to this. You're asking the witness to speculate on something that he's not familiar with, and the fact that he recognises or sees the letter as authentic doesn't mean that he's in a position to explain it. On the other hand, it stands on its own for what it's worth, and Mr. Hannis takes the same objection as we sustained in relation to Mr. Petrovic's objection. Now, can you point to a difference between what you're trying to do here and what the objection was before?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it just seemed to me that part of this document confirms what the general had stated before. Well, anyway, I can move on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the only way I think you can get from him anything that will help you on the question of 50 percent is to ask him if he knows the reason why the 2.500 were rejected. We have here an explanation for the 50 percent being rejected, but what I don't know at the moment is whether he can help us on the reason for the two and a half thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, if you were to give a summary of the reasons for rejecting a number of volunteers, what would you say? What were these reasons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, just before you do that, it's pointed out to me, as I should have noticed, that this wasn't a question of rejection; this was a question of 50 percent giving up, saying they were not ready to obey orders. Now, that's different, in fact, from the question of being rejected by the reception centre. So there isn't a link between these on the face of it, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I'm the one who's wrong; then I will move on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not preventing you asking the witness if he can amplify on the reasons for the 2.500; that's a separate matter, but it doesn't seem to have a direct bearing on this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now when I look at the document I have to accept that. Viewing the document per se, it already reflects what the witness had testified about. So I need -- I see no need to dwell on it any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The next document that I wish to show you, General, is 3D490, the telegram of the 4th of May, 1999. General, I don't know whether you have the document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's the one dated the 26th of April --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, it's 3D490. It should be the 4th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's now on the screen. It will need to be magnified in the Serb for the witness to be able to read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 4th of May, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The 4th of May, 1999. In this document, the Supreme Command Staff cautions against some abuse of weapons on the part of reservists and troops. Are you aware of what happened in terms of the first paragraph of this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After returning from Kosovo, that is the 7th of June, 1999, we had examples of that nature, of such cases, that is. Military conscripts who, objectively speaking, were not capable of carrying out their duties or behaved improperly. So there are several such individual cases, but I know of them after having returned from Kosovo; that is to say, when we received reports, these were the individual cases that I spoke of, starting with individuals who had done something up to two or three reservists or volunteers. That is to say, that such things did occur. Now what is pointed out once again is a reaction to such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Precisely. That was my question. Does this document constitute the right kind of response on the part of the Supreme Command Staff by way of prevention and by way of reaction?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this gives rise to the question as to how, in spite of all the warnings of the Supreme Command Staff that were sent - and so far I've been shown three or four such documents - nevertheless, such persons managed to get through to be among the volunteers down there. So all of it was said, but again you can see that there were individual cases like this one; either procedure in terms of taking in volunteers was not observed or they were not capable of establishing what the situation of a certain individual was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If we look at the last part of this document, we see who it was sent to and we also have a seal, a stamp, that shows the date when this document was sent. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document that I wish to show you is P1490, an order of the Supreme Command Staff of the 26th of April, 1999. If we have a look at paragraph 1 of this document, or rather, the preamble, it says that the Supreme Command Staff had sent several warnings with regard to prohibiting the existence and activities of possible paramilitary formations and so on and so forth. They are enumerated here. My question is as follows: The Supreme Command Staff is aware of the importance of this question; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I could add that I'm not aware of the presence of classical paramilitary formations; that is to say, formations that put on uniforms on their own, formed groups without being subordinated to anyone in Kosovo. There were no such units. Volunteers should not be confused with paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with you. Now, when we look at this order from 1 to 4, in addition to the part that pertains to the possible presence of undesired paramilitary formations, a reference is also made to observing certain rules of the law of war and the Geneva Conventions. And in paragraph 3, documents are referred to that should be the basic documents for that. As for paragraph 3, are those are the documents that you received when you were issued with your equipment? When you were re-activated, you said that you got a set of documents.
