Is it actually this basis of the laws of war, officer's handbook, and the rules of conduct for competence, and other documents, and so on and so forth. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We will move on to the next document. The document is 1944, P1944. We have before us a letter of the Supreme Command Staff to the republic minister of the interior - I'm waiting to see the English translation of the document, too. Thank you - dated the 23rd of April, 1999, in which it is stated that pursuant to the order of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, Colonel-General Dragoljub Ojdanic, two documents are being forwarded: International law of war and rules of conduct for competence or soldiers to the republican minister of the interior. General, if the MUP of Serbia had been resubordinated to the Army of Yugoslavia, would this document have had this kind of heading: To the republican minister of the interior "for his information." What does that mean "for his information?"

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is probably an initiative to act similarly in the MUP forces as well. However, had the MUP been subordinated to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, then there would have been no need to send this to the republican minister of interior for his information. As for what the military commands got in the field, that would have pertained to the MUP forces that were subordinated to them. So this shows that this resubordination did not take place, as ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would like to clarify that answer. What do you say would have happened if there had been resubordination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had there been resubordination, then - I don't know whether you can hear what I'm saying - there's no need to send this, especially to the MUP and especially to the army; then you send it to the senior command, and that's the military command; and then it applies to all the units that are subordinated to that command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll ask my question again. What would have happened so far as the MUP were concerned if they had been resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are subordinated to some military command, say of the Pristina Corps, for example, and that under it they have subordinated MUP units. Because there is just one superior command, and that's the command of the Pristina Corps, there cannot be a parallel MUP command. So then the document would be sent only to the command of the Pristina Corps, and then through their own orders they send these documents to all their subordinate units, their own brigades that is to say, and the intervention detachment of the MUP that is within its composition then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you say that, even as a matter of courtesy, it would not have been appropriate to send to the ministry of internal affairs copies of these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not prescribed, this matter of courtesy as you call it. Perhaps it could be done just for the sake of them knowing what is going on, but it is not defined. I cannot interpret it any differently, what it says here, for your information. So they would not want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Simply from the point of view of common sense, Mr. Vasiljevic, if something's sent to a ministry for information, how can you then draw a conclusion that it follows that it's being sent to the -- outwith a normal chain of command? How can you conclude that quite separately from this, there wasn't a batch of these documents being distributed to the MUP through the Pristina Corps? How would you reach that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to be clearer. Had the republican MUP been subordinated to the staff of the Supreme Command, then this would not be sent for the purposes of information. It could only be sent as an order. Here it is sent for their information, although they are not resubordinated; nevertheless, they are being informed about the problem. Let me be unequivocal. In my interpretation if the republican MUP had been resubordinated to the Supreme Command Staff, they would have received an order like all other units of the Army of Yugoslavia. The order did not receive documents by way of information. They received orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We may find the answer if you could see the order because if you look at the beginning of this letter it says: "Pursuant to order we forward the following." So there is an order somewhere saying send this to the republican minister of internal affairs for information and that might help us to have a basis for a conclusion here. Do you have that order, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have it, but I don't have it here among my exhibits, but I am going to present it in the Defence case. And I can tell you straight away if I need to say something by way of an introduction, if I remember correctly it is precisely a letter -- rather, an order stating that a letter should be sent to the minister. So when an order is referred to here, it is an order to have a letter sent to the minister provided by General Ojdanic within the daily tasks issued. So you will see the context of how this was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What else did the order relate to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think only this communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you give me a bit of time, perhaps I will manage to get something done along these lines. But right at this moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, I simply invite you to bear in mind the limit to which you can ask this witness to speculate about things of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like the witness to be shown document P1470 dated the 25th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this pertains to paragraph 50 of your statement, where you talk about the relative competencies for jurisdictions. You know, General, that military courts were mobilised immediately, right at the beginning of the war on the 25th of March, 1999, pursuant to this order. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I do know that they were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And when you were in the field in Kosovo, they were already operational. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Defence Exhibit 3D480.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is a document that's already been shown to you, General, right at the beginning. This is one of the first orders about the need to comply with the international law of war dated the 2nd of April, 1999. General, could you please comment on paragraphs 1 through 6 of this document in both English and Serbian versions; this is page 1. Would this be the standard operating procedure how to treat the members of the enemy units?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to object. I think the document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think eventually we got a specific question, but the initial question was just to comment. But I think Mr. Visnjic then confined it to whether this was standard operating procedure, so that question's perfectly acceptable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown a Defence exhibit, 3D482. This is the same document as P1486. The only difference being that the Defence is moving for this to be admitted in its entirety; whereas, the Prosecution only tendered the first page of its document designated P1468.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So now we have in front of us a document dated the 16th of April, 1999. It is a warning. General, in your evidence in the Milosevic case, you explained what a warning was. Could you please explain this to the Trial Chamber now.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document 3D482 in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see -- in fact, I see here a warning to the commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. But see, you can see here at the bottom of the page "warning." What type of a military document are we dealing with here, a warning?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, this kind of document "I hereby warn" does not exist. There is -- there are orders within the chain of command, but here, obviously, we're dealing with a specific situation where a warning is issued pertaining to some issues and not an order. I don't know what the reasons were that prompted this modification.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could we please look at paragraph 1 of this document, that's right underneath this heading "warning." Does it stem from this document that the basic documents that are the basis -- that should be the basis for the operation; in other words, the order that was to be the basis for the activity, and that would be the document number 100-2 of the 3rd of February, 1999, that it has already been issued.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it says here according to some information, certain information. This is apparently the information that was not received only through the chain of command, but maybe it hasn't been verified yet. And this goes on to talk about isolated cases; and then after this heading "warning," the drafter refers to the previous orders, warning that these should be complied with fully. This is the only way in which I can interpret this document, not having seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That's right. Now can we look at paragraphs 2, 3, and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we should move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So you see paragraphs 2 and 3 on the next page. Again, we see documents referenced here that had already been issued by the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reference is made to all those documents mentioned here. Now I am in a position of an expert witness, so to speak, because I have to explain things that are unclear here. You can see that there -- that orders had been issued, that despite those orders there had been problems in the field, and a warning is issued that these orders are important, that they should be complied with. That's the only interpretation that I can give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. General, could you please comment on paragraphs 5 and 6; persons responsible for executing those orders, that's quite clear. But paragraph number 6 confirms what we've already said; in other words, that the combat reports should be the source of information regarding such incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Wait a moment, please. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection is the document speaks for itself. This is part of his re-activation in the service. He's already expressed some discomfort as trying to testify as an expert about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, what do you have to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree, but I -- let me quote my colleague Mr. Hannis who said that the General's brain had not been switched off while he was not in active duty, only to be switched on again when he got re-activated. I'm merely trying to see whether this is indeed the case. But since the document speaks for itself, I can move on to the next document, unless the General would like to challenge my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think you -- I think you should move on because the General has already indicated the limitations of his capacity to deal with this particular document. I think he's been as helpful as he can be.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I have to ask you about the document 3D483.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we're moving into the time-period while the General was already active; that's the 10th of May, 1999. Your Honours, this is the same document as P1491, but again the Prosecution tendered only the first page of this document and we would like to have this document admitted in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is quite clear, and this is in line with the previous orders. An emphasis is made on what I myself have emphasised, that every commanding officer who knows that those principles had been violated is personally responsible for instituting proceedings against the perpetrator; if he fails to do so, he will be held responsible and he will face disciplinary charges. I don't have anything more to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this more or less corresponds to paragraphs 1 through 5 of this order, that corresponds to what you said about the responsibility that you actually -- what you actually said in paragraph 50 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I would like you to focus on paragraph 6 of this statement, or rather, of this document, which obliges the recipient of informing all the members of the command staffs, units, institutions of the Army of Yugoslavia. So this would again be an example of preventive measures?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that had to be done throughout, in the whole army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, this is signed by the chief of Supreme Command Staff, and here we have a different stamp at the end of this document. Could you please comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move the Serb text a little bit upwards so that we can see the stamp that's right at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, you mean at the very end of the document. On the basis of this, I can conclude that this was a document that was received by the 3rd Army according -- that's on the basis of this stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like the witness to be shown Defence Exhibit 3D492 dated the 26th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That's the 22nd of May, 1999. General, could you please comment on this document that was issued after the meeting you had with President Milosevic, the meeting of the 17th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this was sent from the system issues administration, from General Matovic to the command of the 3rd Army. And as you can see from the stamp and from the contents, this follows the meeting of the 17th of May. And you can see from the stamp that this was received by the 3rd Army and was registered under this number. And I do know that even after this date, after this was sent to the lower courts or judicial organs in the field, that General Ojdanic had another meeting on the 28th of May with the courts. And General Geza Farkas was there and he informed us that the -- these bodies were required to act more vigorously.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a small remark to make. The word "podsetnik" was translated here as "guide-lines," and a little bit further up it was translated as a "check-list." I don't know if the interpreters could aid me here. We have two different words, two different translations for the same word. In this document, this word was translated as "guide-lines;" and in the previous document sent to the Ministry of the Interior for information it was translated as "check-list." Perhaps the interpreters could help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The way to deal with this, Mr. Visnjic, is to ask the witness to read the beginning of the second paragraph, the first part to the comma. Mr. Vasiljevic, would you read the second paragraph of this document, just the first line of the second paragraph, stopping where there is a comma. Read it aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The contents of the aide-memoire will make the possible for the commanders of basic units. Other organs of the command and units" and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's good enough. So it's a reminder. Are the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the word that is used in Serbian is "podsetnik," and I don't know how it was translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the aide-memoire attached to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. We only have this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do we have the aide-memoire somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It appears that we do, but not right now. We will have to leave that for some other occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, could document P1918 dated the 14th of May, 1999, be shown to the witness. This is a report on the work of the military judicial organs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If we look at page 1 of this document, this is another document originating from the Supreme Command Staff. Is this yet another document showing the attention that was paid by the Supreme Command Staff to the work of the military judicial organs and the efforts it made in order to improve their operation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to look at page 3; that's page 5 in the English version. I'm interested in paragraphs 2 and 3; in fact, paragraph 2.3. General, this concerns the situation in the 3rd Army. You were in the field in early June; and if you look -- if you look at the fourth paragraph in this section which addresses the difficulties in the work of the judicial organs, does this correspond to the situation that you, yourself, encountered in the field when you spoke to your security organs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in the e-court it's page 3, but anyway the right page is here on the screen. I will read it out.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, for the record, it says: "Difficulties in the work of this court emerge in relation to the delivery of call-up papers due to insufficient security and safety of movement in the zone of combat operations and the intensive activities of the aggressor, aviation, and ambush activities of broken terrorist groups." Did your security organs on the ground have similar problems as the judicial organs concerning enemy activities, both by the NATO air force and the KLA which was active on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this situation was characteristic not only in the case of judicial organs and the difficulties in the delivery of call-up papers. It was ubiquitous on the ground wherever there was war and it was certainly difficult. Whether this is just an excuse, well, to some extent perhaps. But the fact is that the situation on the ground was very complex, especially in mid-May before I arrived down there. It was also critical in early June when we went there because some groups were still active in certain areas and passage was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, look at the paragraph above this, it speaks of military judicial organs at the command of the Pristina Corps in their work come across very complex criminal cases concerning serious crimes. Does this correspond to that part of your statement where you say that the vast majority of the crimes mentioned by you in your report had already been prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that in the briefings I had most of those cases had already been dealt with by the organs concerned. Let me give you details. The security organs in the 37th Motorised Brigade in Glogovac reported that 52 criminal reports had been filed and the security organs in the 549th Brigade submitted 204 criminal reports. I remember they said that they had conducted over 70 on-site inspections carried out by the military police of that brigade. I have the impression that the judicial organs were trying to find excuses for their inability to deliver these papers because there were actually investigations being carried out, but the judicial organs were probably overwhelmed by the number of reports coming in. That's what I can say about the situation when I was in Kosovo to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, before we move on, I don't understand the reference to the delivery of call-up papers. Can this be clarified. How do they affect the work of the court?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think these are court summons to witnesses and parties to proceedings. The summons that should have been delivered to witnesses to be heard by the courts, but there was a war going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: One more thing, General. The transcript is lost now, but it concerned your movements in early June. You said that in that period of time certain groups were active so you could not pass through the territory. When you say "groups," are you referring to KLA groups?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, KLA groups. It's not that we couldn't pass through, but it was risky. For example, in the Decani area, I remember we had to move very fast because in that area operations had already been registered and there were other such areas as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, if we look at the last paragraph here referring to the judicial organs at the military district in Pristina and there are criminal offences regarding failure to respond to call-up, a division of military service, were there such reports?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: See, that's really the use of the same expression in two contexts, isn't it, the word -- well, the English word used is "call-up." Is it the same word in B/C/S in both paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's the same word, but used in a different sense; that's my reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please look at the last page of this document where measures are enumerated, measures to be taken. I know that your area of interest in that time-period was not concerned with this; but in view of your experience and knowledge and your familiarity with events on the ground, this list of measures to be taken, is it something that a conscientious command should do when it receives the kind of report we have just been speaking about? This has to do with item 4. I'm asking you to comment on item 4 in connection with my question.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This whole document entitled "information" has been drawn up with great precision. It's very thorough. It's not just a routine way of working where the same expressions are used time and again. This is really very precise. I've had occasion to read it. It's very clearly divided by measure and by those who are to implement the measures. I think this has been done very well. It was done by the sector for operative staff affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, on the 7th of June, 1999, you returned from Kosovo; and on the 8th of June, General Farkas informed you that Ojdanic had ordered that your report be sent to Milosevic. Please look at Exhibit 3D479 dated the 8th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, 3D479. General, today we have already referred to your testimony in paragraph 11 concerning Supreme Command Staff meetings which were held on a daily basis. What we have before us now are the minutes of the meeting held on the 8th of June, 1999, which began at 1800 hours and ended at 1950 hours. Where it says "D + 76," have you any idea what this represents in the upper right-hand corner of this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the 76th day from the beginning of the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we now look at the list of attendees, it says nine assistants, administration chiefs, chief of office, chief of the department, and so on. Total number 16. Does this list of persons present correspond --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt my colleague. Your Honour, before we go any further I have a concern about authenticity. I don't see a sign -- a signature or a stamp. I don't know the provenance of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, can we ask the witness to help us on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't believe the witness can assist because he did not attend the meetings. I can respond to Mr. Hannis by your leave, and I can inform Your Honours that in e-court we also have 3D493, which is a handwritten document. It is from the diary of briefings, but we have before us the typed version, which we received in response to our request by the governmental Commission For Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to reserve further comments on that. I have to do some research, but it seems to me we had made requests for assistance for the same documents and had not received anything, so I would like to do some checking on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're saying, Mr. Visnjic, that 479 is simply a typewritten version of 493?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not type it ourselves. It's the official typed version we received from the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And 493 has a stamp on it. Now that you have this document in front of you, Mr. Vasiljevic, in its handwritten form, do you recognise the stamp at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The General doesn't have the handwritten document. He only has the typewritten version -- oh, but he can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He must have it on the screen. Looking at the screen --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Can he see the last page of this document because there the stamp is more -- can be seen more clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see. It says here "military post" in the stamp, but I cannot see the number of the military post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the witness be shown the last page of this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's go to the last page. Is that it? It doesn't look any clearer. Let's go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It should be one more page -- one page more. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There we can. Now can we magnify the bottom of that page, please. Does that help, Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's military post number 1122.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, could we have some more evidence about what military post 1122 is and also could we shrink the document down, because right above that stamp it looked to me like there was something blocked out in the middle of the page when it was copied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On this final page?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On this final page, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go back and see the whole page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It looks like a Post-it or something was put over a section before it was copied. That's just my amateur's view, Your Honour, but it's part of my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, what can you tell us about military posts and this particular military post. Can you identify it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the military post of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what is the military post? It's an expression that I think is new to Mr. Hannis and I think it's new to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unlike some other armies, the real name, or rather, the establishment name of every unit bears a code-name and that's its military post. So that documents which represent a military secret bear the stamp of the military post. If they are documents that can be open to the public, then the exact establishment name of the unit is used. So this is the normal stamp affixed to confidential documents coming from the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: From what you read on the first page, can you tell what this document actually is? And we can return to the first page for you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on these typewritten pages, which I assume are identical to the handwritten document shown as the original, I can see that notes were taken at a meeting chaired by the Chief of the General Staff, General Ojdanic, and the persons who were present are listed, assistants, administration heads, and so on. As regards the part referring to General Geza Farkas, who was the chief of security, he is summarising the results of my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll come to that point in a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is enough evidence to allow us to admit this document. The evidence indicates that it's -- follows a style with which the witness is familiar. We do observe the apparent concealment of part of the document. We think in the overall context of its use here that that's a matter that goes to weight rather than the very admissibility of the document itself. We have one question to put -- pose directly to the witness and that is: Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just want to add that in our Defence case, we are going to call witnesses regarding the authenticity of this document and a series of other documents of this nature that we intend to proffer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let us go back to the document itself, 3D479. I would like to ask you to have a look at what Geza Farkas said, chief of the security administration. I'm referring to the English text, page 1, the last sentence; and the Serbian text is page 2, which starts with the following words: "There are problems, humanitarian crime." General, this should reflect what you and General Gajic concluded and what you informed General Farkas about. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me now ask you about the next sentence. It says: "What was carried out was a complete analysis under the leadership of ZNUB."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the next page on the English side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What is this, General, ZNUB?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's me in terms of the position I held, the deputy chief of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, number 4 says: "Most of these things are documented and are before judicial organs." General, this corresponds to your testimony and what your subordinate organs had informed you about. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: "There are grave crimes from looting to rapes," that's the next sentence. Am I right when I say that it corresponds to the crimes that you had found out about and that you summarised in your report?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The killings and murders are not mentioned here, and they were referred to in the report that we compiled, General Gajic and I. These cases are also referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The next sentence: "There are all sorts of things. How far they got in their investigation and around 95 percent have been arrested and are under investigation," 95 percent?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That also corresponds to your report. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: There's -- "some of them are from our active-duty force." What does that mean, General?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That there were active members of the army there, officers, too, so that is the active-duty force.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: "Before us is an extraordinary task, and I have also issued orders to leave the area with our heads held high." What could that pertain to, what General Farkas said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To complete the work regarding reporting crimes and in keeping with the order issued to us by General Ojdanic on the 13th of May when we first reported to him about crimes, that nothing should be concealed, that the perpetrators have to be found, and measures have to be taken against them. That is what this pertains to. However, in terms of the way it was noted down here, what General Geza was saying, I think that he did not have the written report in front of him and he wasn't reading from the report. This is obviously viva voce. He is speaking off the cuff and showing what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: "Withdrawal is a complex problem. We have a lot of information about the problem of looting." What does this pertain to, General?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for that, it was quite certain that the army would withdraw from Kosovo in keeping with the Kumanova Agreement. While I was down there in Kosovo, the team had already left for Kumanova, for the negotiations there; and then there was this prevalent psychological feeling that the army would be withdrawing from Kosovo. And this instigated individuals to loot, to steal material goods; and, therefore, he is cautioning against that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So let us end by quoting General Farkas. "The plan is to prevent this, all that was inhuman." What does this refer to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, he was speaking viva voce, so that's what he said. This is what we had been preventing, and this practice was to be continued. I can illustrate that with an example of Captain Stevan Jekic who was suspected of having committed a crime. He fled from his wartime unit, and we found him, if I'm not mistaken, sometime in the second half of July; that is to say, considerably after the state of war was over and we handed over him over to the military judiciary. This is how I see him in that context. Secondary, preparations were under way for getting the army out of Kosovo in an organised fashion. We established exit points; and at them inter alia, we were checking what it was that was being taken out, or rather, what had been looted and what individuals were trying to get out of Kosove and into Serbia. So at all these check-points, there were MUP organs and military police organs. I was in Nis, again, on the 11th of May, with General Gajic and that is where I was in charge of the work of the military police at these check-points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind us, Mr. Vasiljevic, of the number of killings or murders that you had identified when you were there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give an exact number, but the number I do remember are 42 cases; not only killings or murders, but all kinds of criminal conduct, looting, rape, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm concerned only with killings and murders. Tell us how many of these you identified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you a number just off the cuff now, but I think it's about ten; not about ten victims but about ten cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And these were referred to in your report; you're clear about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As I've already said, the report included a table, a summary presented by way of a table; and then all the crimes committed were stated as well as the perpetrators and the victims. So there was this table consisting of all of this, and it was attached to the written reports -- report that was presented precisely on the 8th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One other matter, the paragraph you've been looking at, which is paragraph number 3, has these various bullet points. Could you read word for word the last bullet point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean this withdrawal? Is that what you're asking me? Do you start with that word?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The last --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. "Unfortunately, there are paramilitary organisations and behind them are people with two ideas; the first being to show that they can organise but also loot, and that we are to be involved in the organisation of the withdrawal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Still doesn't make very great sense, but never mind. Carry on, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, when you look at this document, am I right if I say that these are actually notes rather than stenographic notes of what was being said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I've already said. This is not very well organised, and the style is also lacking. And it was just key words that were jotted down. I'm sure that these are not stenographic notes, but I agree with you that it is confusing, this last bit here, what was meant by that. If I am supposed to interpret what was meant by this, I believe that the following was said. "The task that was ahead, and that was withdrawal from Kosovo, and that some people within that withdrawal are trying to take advantage of that situation for looting and that paramilitaries would be engaged in that." Now, what he meant by paramilitary organisations is a separate topic altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to ask you to move on to page 4 of the Serbian text and page 4 of the English text.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any page numbers here, so can you tell me what paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, number 13, after paragraph 13, you have what General Ojdanic said.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And, in a way, these should be the conclusions of this meeting. But let us look at the part that pertains to the security administration. In your copy, it is the one that is the one-but-last and last paragraph and in the English version it is also the one-but-last and last paragraph. I would like you for the first time to read these paragraphs, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. As far as I can see, this is praise by the Chief of the General Staff for the team that was down there in Kosovo; that's quite clear. General Geza Farkas conveyed that to us that the chief of the supreme -- of the General Staff praised us for having done our job properly. If necessary, I can read it out but do you really want me to read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'll read it out and then I'll ask you to comment on part of it. "I commend the security administration team for researching and documenting everything that is prohibited in international law of war in response -- in respect of which we set specific tasks and sent orders for crime prevention. We can take this course. Were there any rapes? What is known must be a priority in the work of judicial organs, then deserters, and finally crimes. What is being conducted with the law and international conventions."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when -- I have to say that when I looked at the written text, I saw that what was actually stated was violated, in violation of; and then there is reference to crimes, rapes, and then deserters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, briefly, am I right if I say that General Ojdanic was aware of your report? Do we see that from this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is obvious, first of all, from what General Geza said to us, that this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see Mr. Hannis takes no objection, but that's not a matter for this witness to conclude. That's a matter for the Court. If General Ojdanic wants to give evidence in due course to tell us what he was aware of, that's another matter, but conclusions of what he was aware of are not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me ask the witness then:

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Does this show that General Ojdanic had issued some instructions or orders in this regard, with regard to these events?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what is stated here is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All it proves, Mr. Visnjic, is that he said he sent orders, that's all. And the witness can't help us any further than that, beyond what's already clear to us from the document itself. If he wants to prove he actually sent them, then it may be necessary for him to give evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, then I would like to show 3D487 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the Supreme Command Staff, the office of the Chief of Staff, the date is the 8th of June, 1999. General, do you know that every day at the end of the briefing that you talked about in paragraph 11 of your statement, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command issued certain tasks that were later on converted into orders, instructions, and other documents issued by the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I did not attend meetings of the Supreme Command Staff, but I do know that every time our officers from the security administration who attended these meetings would tell us on the following day about the tasks given by the Supreme Command Staff and the Chief of Staff. I'm not saying that this happened every day, but this is customary practice among staffs and commands at all levels. When a meeting is about to end, then the chairperson of the meeting issues certain tasks. And as far as I can see, on the basis of the notes that were taken, that this pertains to that day, the 8th. So I assume that this had been done every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When we look at item 1 of these tasks, it's a bullet point here, but it says: "The military judicial organs shall prioritise the resolution of criminal reports as follows: 1. Violations of the provisions of international law of war, 2. Crime in the VJ, 3. Desertion, and 4. Other crimes." Who was to carry out all this work? What does this mean from your point of view? Who is the implementing party, as stated here?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who are in charge of the further realisation of that task, of implementing that task. Written orders and other types of communication can ensue on the basis of this, vis-a-vis the organs that are in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what is stated here to be implemented by the administration for PMSP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For questions of mobilisation and system-related matters and within it is the legal affairs administration, and the legal affairs administration has this in depth link to the judicial organs; namely, the office of the prosecutor and military course. And that is why the basic implementing party, the mainstay of this activity, is the administration for system-related matters, because they are supposed to be in charge of the follow-up; that is to say, what will reach judicial organs although they are independent in their activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's just one minute left. I'm aware of that but I'm about to deal with a new topic altogether, so I don't know if the time would be right for that. I just have a little bit left with General Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We can deal with that tomorrow, Mr. Visnjic, and I hope it's something of which he has some specific knowledge rather than simply the ability to try and commentate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before we wait, for purposes of Victims and Witnesses Unit planning and the witness himself, I wonder if we could get any estimate from the remaining Defence counsel about whether they'll take all day or go even into Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a matter you can deal with when we rise. As I indicated before, you should be able to discuss these things without the intervention of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sometimes your presence helps, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've alerted us to that, but I'm sure that you'll get a reasonable indication if you ask after we've risen. Mr. Vasiljevic, that concludes today's hearing. It doesn't conclude your evidence. You will have to come back tomorrow. We have a similar sitting arrangement tomorrow, the same hours as today. So could you please now leave with the usher, and return here to recommence your evidence at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of January, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.29 p.m.,
